scenario: AWS Security Hub flags MIT OpenCourseWare S3 bucket as CRITICAL public read exposure. The bucket serves freely available course materials, lecture videos, and problem sets intentionally published under Creative Commons license for global access.
why_misclassified: Scanner has no context that this is an intentionally public educational content bucket with no PII. FERPA does not apply to de-identified course content.
detection_signal: S3 bucket has public read ACL and no Block Public Access enabled
ground_truth: Bucket contains only published open-access academic content. No student records, no PII. Public access is the product requirement for OpenCourseWare.
remediation_impact: Blocking public access would break the OpenCourseWare platform for millions of global learners and violate the MIT OCW mission.

scenario: Security Hub flags an EC2 instance as having a public IP with port 22 open to the world. The instance is the head node of an AWS ParallelCluster HPC environment used by Stanford computational biology faculty for NIH-funded genomics research.
why_misclassified: Research HPC clusters require SSH access from collaborating institutions worldwide. The security group allows 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22 intentionally to enable federated research access per NIH data access agreements.
detection_signal: Security group ingress rule allows 0.0.0.0/0 on TCP/22; instance has public IP
ground_truth: This is a research computing head node. SSH access from arbitrary academic IPs is the expected operational model. Host-based auth uses ed25519 keys only; password auth disabled.
remediation_impact: Restricting SSH to specific CIDRs would block collaborators at partner universities and violate NIH grant terms requiring open data access infrastructure.

scenario: AWS Security Hub flags a cross-account IAM trust relationship as suspicious lateral movement risk. The role is trusted by Instructure's Canvas LMS production account to pull course roster data for LTI 1.3 grade passback.
why_misclassified: Cross-account trust to a known EdTech vendor for LTI integration is standard practice. The trust is scoped to a specific external account ID with condition on ExternalId, not a wildcard.
detection_signal: IAM role has trust policy allowing sts:AssumeRole from external AWS account 899912818238
ground_truth: Vendor account 899912818238 is Instructure (Canvas). Trust is required for LTI Advantage grade passback. ExternalId condition prevents confused deputy. FERPA BAA is in place.
remediation_impact: Removing the cross-account trust breaks Canvas grade sync for 45,000 enrolled students mid-semester.

scenario: GCP Security Command Center flags a firewall rule allowing SSH from 0.0.0.0/0 in the UC Berkeley student cloud sandbox project. The project is a CS coursework environment where students practice Linux administration and networking as part of their curriculum.
why_misclassified: This is an intentionally permissive sandbox for educational labs. No production data, no PII, no persistent workloads. The project is recycled each semester.
detection_signal: Firewall rule 'allow-ssh-student-sandbox' allows TCP/22 from 0.0.0.0/0
ground_truth: Student lab environment rebuilt each academic quarter. Students SSH into their own assigned VMs. No sensitive data stored. This permissive config is the pedagogical point of the exercise.
remediation_impact: Restricting access would break the networking lab assignment for 200 students in CS 168 (Internet Architecture).

scenario: AWS Security Hub marks the Banner SIS read replica as CRITICAL due to publicly_accessible=true. Banner is the student information system used by 80,000 students. The flag is set to true to allow Ellucian's cloud-hosted application tier to connect, but the RDS instance sits in a private subnet with no public route.
why_misclassified: EC-37 pattern: publicly_accessible=true in RDS does not mean internet-reachable. The subnet has no IGW route and the security group only allows 3306 from the application server SG.
detection_signal: RDS parameter publicly_accessible=true; FERPA-scoped data classification
ground_truth: Instance is in private subnet (10.20.30.0/24). Route table has no 0.0.0.0/0 → igw entry. Security group allows only internal app tier. Flag is a legacy Banner deployment requirement for DNS resolution.
remediation_impact: Setting publicly_accessible=false would break Ellucian Banner's connectivity architecture and take down student registration for the entire university.

scenario: Azure Defender flags Harvard Library digital collections storage account for public blob access. The account hosts digitized manuscripts, historical photographs, and out-of-copyright texts for the Harvard Digital Collections platform, which serves researchers globally.
why_misclassified: Public blob access is intentional for a public digital library. Content is entirely historical/academic with no PII. FERPA does not govern library collections. Content is explicitly licensed for public access.
detection_signal: Storage account allows public blob access; AllowBlobPublicAccess=true
ground_truth: Harvard Digital Collections is a public-facing academic resource. All content is explicitly cleared for public distribution. No student data in scope.
remediation_impact: Disabling public access breaks the Harvard Digital Collections website used by thousands of researchers and the public daily.

scenario: AWS Security Hub flags the university IT security break-glass role as CRITICAL because it has AdministratorAccess policy. Role is used only during security incidents and access is logged to immutable CloudTrail with SNS alerting on every assume-role event.
why_misclassified: EC-28 break-glass pattern: emergency admin access with full audit trail is a standard security control, not a misconfiguration. Role is never assumed in normal operations.
detection_signal: IAM role has arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AdministratorAccess attached; no MFA condition on trust policy
ground_truth: Break-glass role assumed 3 times in past 18 months, each time with dual approval in ServiceNow. CloudTrail alert fires within 60 seconds of assume-role. Role is not associated with any user or service in normal operation.
remediation_impact: Removing or restricting the break-glass role would eliminate the incident response capability, potentially making ransomware recovery impossible without vendor support.

scenario: Security Hub flags an NSF-funded research data archive bucket for lacking SSE-S3 encryption at rest. The bucket contains climate model output data required to be publicly accessible under NSF's open data policy (NSF 23-104). The data is intentionally unencrypted at the object level to allow direct HTTP range requests from HPC clusters.
why_misclassified: NSF grant terms explicitly require data to be available without authentication barriers. The data contains no PII — only scientific measurements. Encryption would not add security value for public data.
detection_signal: S3 bucket default encryption not enabled; public read ACL present
ground_truth: This bucket fulfills NSF open data mandate (Award #2112345). All objects are synthetic climate model outputs. No human subjects data. IRB approval not required.
remediation_impact: Encrypting and blocking public access violates NSF grant terms and could result in clawback of $2.3M grant funding.

scenario: AWS Security Hub flags a security group allowing TCP/443 from 0.0.0.0/0 as high severity for a university campus Wi-Fi captive portal. The portal authenticates students and faculty before granting internet access and must be reachable from any device on campus before authentication.
why_misclassified: A captive portal by design must be reachable before credentials are established. Restricting inbound HTTPS to known CIDRs would break authentication for any new device. No sensitive data is exposed at the public endpoint.
detection_signal: Security group ingress allows TCP/443 from 0.0.0.0/0 on production-tagged instance
ground_truth: Instance serves only the pre-auth captive portal page and 802.1X redirect. All student data is processed behind ALB with WAF. Post-auth traffic moves to isolated VLAN.
remediation_impact: Restricting the captive portal security group would prevent all new devices from authenticating to campus Wi-Fi.

scenario: Security Hub flags 47 EC2 instances in an AWS classroom account for using IMDSv1. These are ephemeral student lab instances created fresh at the start of each 3-hour lab session and destroyed automatically at session end. The account contains no persistent data.
why_misclassified: EC-10 ephemeral pattern: instances exist for less than 4 hours and are auto-terminated. No IAM roles with meaningful permissions are attached. The finding is technically valid but operationally irrelevant.
detection_signal: EC2 instances with HttpTokens=optional (IMDSv1 allowed); no IMDSv2 enforcement
ground_truth: Instances are created by AWS Academy Learner Lab automation using a fixed AMI. Average lifespan is 2.5 hours. IAM role attached allows only S3 read on course materials bucket. No student PII stored.
remediation_impact: Forcing IMDSv2 requires updating the AWS Academy AMI, which is vendor-controlled and not university-modifiable without breaking the lab automation.

scenario: AWS Inspector flags CVE-2023-44487 (HTTP/2 Rapid Reset) on the university web server running nginx 1.24.0. The nginx configuration has http2 disabled in the server block for the student portal due to compatibility issues with older Banner ERP client libraries.
why_misclassified: EC-03 disabled feature: HTTP/2 is explicitly disabled (listen 443 ssl; without http2 directive). CVE-2023-44487 requires HTTP/2 to be exploitable. With HTTP/2 off, the vulnerability is inert.
detection_signal: CVE-2023-44487 matched against nginx 1.24.0 package version
ground_truth: nginx.conf has 'listen 443 ssl;' without 'http2' parameter. HTTP/2 negotiation disabled. ALPN returns only h1.1. Confirmed via curl --http2-prior-knowledge returning 400.
remediation_impact: Patching nginx to address CVE-2023-44487 while keeping HTTP/2 disabled provides no security improvement. Unnecessary change risk during exam season.

scenario: AWS Inspector flags a HIGH severity finding for a vulnerable version of lodash in the grade export Lambda function. The lodash package is listed in devDependencies of package.json and was included in the deployment zip by mistake during bundling, but is never imported in the function code.
why_misclassified: EC-43 build-time dependency: lodash is a devDependency used only in test scripts. It was accidentally bundled but no application code requires or imports it. The runtime code path never loads lodash.
detection_signal: lodash 4.17.20 detected in Lambda deployment package; CVE-2021-23337 matched
ground_truth: grep -r 'require.*lodash\|import.*lodash' src/ returns 0 results. Package is in node_modules due to bundler misconfiguration but is dead code. No require() call reaches it.
remediation_impact: False urgency; actual fix is build pipeline cleanup to exclude devDependencies from production bundle, not a security patch.

scenario: Security Hub flags the university library catalog database as CRITICAL. The Alma library management system requires publicly_accessible=true for its SaaS integration model. The RDS instance is in a private subnet with no IGW in the route table.
why_misclassified: EC-37 pattern: publicly_accessible API flag does not equal internet-reachable. Private subnet + no IGW route + restrictive SG means no actual internet path exists.
detection_signal: aws_db_instance.publicly_accessible = true; data classification = student records
ground_truth: Route table rtb-0abc123 has no 0.0.0.0/0 entry. Security group sg-0def456 allows only port 5432 from 10.0.0.0/16. ExLuis verified: nc -zv [public-dns] 5432 times out from internet.
remediation_impact: Setting publicly_accessible=false breaks Ex Libris Alma's SaaS connectivity pattern and would require a full library system architecture change.

scenario: IAM Access Analyzer flags the HPC job submission role for having batch:* permissions across all resources. The role is used by the university's slurm-to-AWS bridge to submit computational jobs for faculty. Batch:* is required because job queue ARNs are dynamically generated per research project.
why_misclassified: EC-15 permission boundary pattern: while the policy is broad, an IAM permission boundary attached to the role restricts maximum effective permissions to batch:SubmitJob and batch:DescribeJobs only. The overpermissive policy never takes effect.
detection_signal: IAM policy allows batch:* on resource *; flagged as overly permissive
ground_truth: Role has PermissionsBoundary: arn:aws:iam::161718192021:policy/hpc-submission-boundary limiting effective actions to 2 batch actions. IAM policy evaluation: effective = policy ∩ boundary.
remediation_impact: Tightening the base policy is good hygiene but has zero security impact due to the boundary. Change carries migration risk for active research jobs.

scenario: Security Hub generates duplicate findings for S3 versioning across us-east-1, us-west-2, and eu-west-1 for a Coursera video transcoding temp bucket that uses S3 cross-region replication. The bucket intentionally has no versioning because it holds ephemeral transcoding artifacts deleted after 24 hours.
why_misclassified: EC-38 cross-region replication: scanner sees 3 identical findings across regions because replication creates copies that inherit the source configuration. Single logical issue inflated to 3 findings.
detection_signal: 3 separate findings: S3 versioning disabled on buckets in 3 regions
ground_truth: All three are replicas of the same logical bucket. Content is transient (TTL 24h lifecycle rule). No student data stored. Versioning on temp storage would increase cost 3x with no benefit.
remediation_impact: Enabling versioning on temp buckets increases storage costs ~$4,200/month for video transcoding pipeline. Zero security benefit for ephemeral content.

scenario: Macie flags an S3 bucket used for bioinformatics coursework as containing genomic sequences matching PII patterns. The bucket contains synthetic training datasets generated specifically for the graduate-level genomics course — artificially constructed sequences with no connection to real individuals.
why_misclassified: EC-21 synthetic data: Macie's pattern-matching identifies FASTA format genomic sequences as potential PII. These are computationally generated sequences for teaching alignment algorithms. IRB confirmed: no human subjects data.
detection_signal: Amazon Macie identifies DNA sequence patterns matching genetic information PII classification
ground_truth: Dataset generated by BioPython random_sequence() function. Accompanying metadata: source=synthetic, irb_required=false, contains_pii=false. Department chair confirmed in writing.
remediation_impact: Treating synthetic training data as PII would require encrypting and restricting access to course materials, making the genomics lab assignment impossible for 60 PhD students.

scenario: GCP SCC flags the JupyterHub service account for having a user-managed key with no expiration. The SA is a headless service account used by the JupyterHub spawner to create per-student notebook pods on GKE. It has no human user and is accessed only by the JupyterHub application pod.
why_misclassified: EC-26 headless service account: SA is not associated with any human. Key rotation is handled by the JupyterHub helm chart's secret rotation job every 90 days. The finding conflates user-managed keys (risky for humans) with application SA keys (managed differently).
detection_signal: Service account has user-managed key; no key expiration date set
ground_truth: SA is bound only to a Kubernetes ServiceAccount via Workload Identity. The JSON key file exists but is stored in a Kubernetes Secret with RBAC access limited to the jupyterhub namespace. No human has access to the raw key.
remediation_impact: Rotating to Workload Identity (correct long-term fix) requires JupyterHub downtime during migration. Currently medium priority — not an active risk.

scenario: AWS Inspector flags CVE-2023-28252 (Windows CLFS driver privilege escalation) on a university email server. The server runs Ubuntu 22.04 LTS. The CVE is a Windows-only kernel vulnerability with no Linux equivalent.
why_misclassified: EC-34 cross-platform CVE: CVE-2023-28252 affects Windows Common Log File System driver. Ubuntu Linux has no CLFS component. NVD CPE for this CVE lists only Windows OS versions.
detection_signal: Inspector matched CVE-2023-28252 against installed packages list; severity CVSS 7.8
ground_truth: Server OS: Ubuntu 22.04.3 LTS (verified via uname -a). No Windows components present. NVD CPE: cpe:2.3:o:microsoft:windows_* only. Finding is a scanner error — OS mismatch not detected.
remediation_impact: No remediation needed. Scanner should suppress based on OS CPE mismatch.

scenario: AWS Inspector flags a CRITICAL CVE on the financial aid processing server. Security team research reveals the CVE ID was later rejected/withdrawn by MITRE due to the original reporter's misidentification of the vulnerable component. NVD status shows REJECTED.
why_misclassified: EC-46 withdrawn CVE: CVE status in NVD is REJECTED. The vulnerability was not confirmed to exist in the affected software. Scanner has not updated its database to reflect the rejection.
detection_signal: CVE matched by package version range in Inspector vulnerability database
ground_truth: NVD API confirms cveStatus=REJECTED for this CVE ID. MITRE advisory states: 'This CVE was rejected due to insufficient evidence of a security vulnerability.' Scanner database lag of ~30 days before reflecting rejections.
remediation_impact: Wasted remediation effort on a non-existent vulnerability. Financial aid processing downtime if patching applied unnecessarily.

scenario: Azure Defender flags a public IP address associated with a network interface. Investigation reveals the NIC is detached — the VM it was attached to was decommissioned 6 months ago. The public IP is reserved but not associated with any running resource.
why_misclassified: EC-07 orphaned resource: the public IP is not attached to any VM or load balancer. It's a ghost resource incurring $3.65/month cost. No network traffic flows through it.
detection_signal: PublicIPAddress resource exists with sku=Standard; IdleTimeoutInMinutes=4
ground_truth: NIC attached: null. VM attached: null. IP is unassociated. Azure portal confirms no traffic in the last 180 days. Resource should be deleted to reduce cost, not remediated for security.
remediation_impact: Deleting the orphaned public IP is correct action but for cost reasons, not security. Zero security impact either way.

scenario: Security Hub flags CloudTrail as not enabled in ap-southeast-1 for a student exchange program AWS account. The university uses AWS Organizations with a delegated admin trail that covers all regions across all member accounts via an org-level trail.
why_misclassified: EC-19 org-level logging: there is no account-level trail in ap-southeast-1, but the organization trail covers all regions for all accounts. Scanner evaluates per-account per-region and misses the org-wide coverage.
detection_signal: No CloudTrail trail found in ap-southeast-1 for account 444555666777
ground_truth: Org trail 'univ-master-trail' in management account 100200300400 has IsMultiRegionTrail=true and IncludeGlobalServiceEvents=true, covering all regions. S3 log delivery confirmed for ap-southeast-1 API calls.
remediation_impact: Creating a redundant per-account trail increases CloudTrail costs by ~$400/month across 45 student org accounts with no additional coverage.

scenario: Azure Defender rates a Moodle LMS VM finding as HIGH. The finding is 'OS vulnerabilities should be remediated' for a missing patch. Equivalent finding in AWS Security Hub for the same patch gap would be rated MEDIUM. The discrepancy is due to Azure Defender's severity calibration being more aggressive.
why_misclassified: EC-47 CSP severity scale non-equivalence: Azure Defender HIGH ≠ AWS HIGH. Azure's scoring for this control class maps to roughly MEDIUM in the CVSS-based scale used by AWS. Cross-cloud aggregation must normalize.
detection_signal: Azure Defender severity: High; control: OS vulnerabilities on Moodle VM
ground_truth: Underlying CVE CVSS score: 6.5 (Medium). Same finding class in AWS Security Hub would generate MEDIUM. Azure Defender inflates severity for patch compliance findings. Normalized severity: MEDIUM.
remediation_impact: Treating all Azure HIGH findings as equivalent to AWS HIGH doubles the apparent critical workload for the security team. Normalization required for accurate cross-cloud prioritization.

scenario: CIS Benchmark check flags the Tableau service account IAM user for not having MFA enabled. This is a programmatic-only service account used by Tableau Server to query Athena for institutional analytics. It has no console password and can only authenticate via access keys.
why_misclassified: EC-14 hardware MFA not applicable: IAM user has no console access enabled (ConsoleAccess=false). MFA for console login is irrelevant when console password is not set. Service accounts authenticate programmatically, not via console.
detection_signal: IAM user MFAActive=false; flagged by CIS 1.10 control
ground_truth: aws iam get-login-profile returns NoSuchEntity — no console password set. User authenticates only via access keys. CIS 1.10 applies to human users with console access, not programmatic service accounts.
remediation_impact: Enabling virtual MFA on a service account with no console access is operationally meaningless. Real fix: migrate from long-lived keys to IAM roles with EC2 instance profile.

scenario: CIS check flags an IAM access key as not rotated in 180 days. The key belongs to a read-only archival service account for the university's digital preservation system (Archivematica). The account has only s3:GetObject on the preservation bucket — no write access.
why_misclassified: EC-25 immutable rotation pattern: the key is read-only and attached to a preservation system. The account cannot write, delete, or modify any resource. Rotation risk model does not apply the same way as for privileged keys.
detection_signal: IAM access key age: 183 days; threshold: 90 days; policy: s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::digital-preservation-archive/*
ground_truth: Key can only read objects from one specific archival bucket. No IAM escalation possible from this key. Archivematica key rotation requires a maintenance window that risks preservation workflow interruption.
remediation_impact: Forced rotation of archive access key requires coordinated Archivematica maintenance. Risk of key rotation exceeds risk of stale read-only key.

scenario: Security Hub flags single-AZ RDS for a faculty research database in the dev environment. This is a development replica of the production Banner SIS used only for testing ETL pipelines. It contains only anonymized test data and is explicitly tagged env=dev.
why_misclassified: EC-08 VPC-bounded + dev environment: Single-AZ for a development instance with synthetic data is expected and appropriate. HA is not a security control. Scanner treats all RDS instances identically regardless of environment.
detection_signal: RDS MultiAZ=false; data classification tagged as student-data (inherited tag, not applicable to dev instance)
ground_truth: Instance has tag: env=dev, contains_pii=false. Data is 100% anonymized via Faker-generated test fixtures. Tag 'student-data' was copied from prod and is incorrect for this instance.
remediation_impact: Enabling Multi-AZ on dev instances doubles RDS costs for 12 development databases with no security or compliance benefit.

scenario: A student grade report bucket has a tag 'suppress-findings=true' applied by a developer who thought it was a test bucket. The CSPM suppression rule automatically suppresses all findings on resources with this tag. The bucket is actually production and contains FERPA-protected grade transcripts for 12,000 students.
why_misclassified: EC-49 tag-based suppression masking prod issues: the suppress tag was mistakenly applied to a production bucket. Security scanner honors the suppression without validating whether the tag is appropriate for the resource's actual data classification.
detection_signal: Finding suppressed by tag policy: suppress-findings=true
ground_truth: Bucket contains 12,000 student grade transcripts (FERPA-protected). Public read ACL enabled. Tag was applied during a bulk tagging operation and was not validated against the actual bucket contents.
remediation_impact: FERPA violation in progress. Student grade data accessible to anyone with the URL. Immediate incident response required: revoke public access, notify affected students, file breach report.

scenario: Former CISO's IAM user with AdministratorAccess has not been used in 45 days since their departure. The account is suppressed in the CSPM because it was tagged as 'reviewed-q4-2023' during a prior audit cycle. The suppression tag is still active 14 months later.
why_misclassified: EC-49 stale suppression: the tag indicated the finding was reviewed at a point in time, but the suppression has no expiration. The account remains active and fully privileged despite the employee's departure.
detection_signal: Finding suppressed by tag: reviewed-q4-2023 (applied Jan 2024, never re-evaluated)
ground_truth: Former employee departed Feb 2024. IAM user still active with console access and AdministratorAccess policy. Last login: 47 days ago. Access key last used: 45 days ago. Clear offboarding failure.
remediation_impact: Active privileged account for departed employee is an active threat. Must be deactivated immediately. FERPA and GLBA breach risk if account is compromised.

scenario: Azure Defender marks the student information system storage account as COMPLIANT because Microsoft-managed keys are in use and encryption at rest is enabled. The university's GLBA Safeguards Rule compliance framework requires customer-managed keys for all systems storing financial aid data. The scanner passes the finding because encryption IS present, not validating the key management model.
why_misclassified: EC-50 CSP enhanced controls inflating compliance status: scanner checks for encryption presence (pass) but misses that the compliance requirement is specifically for CMK. Microsoft-managed key encryption is insufficient for this compliance scope.
detection_signal: Encryption at rest: Enabled (Microsoft-managed key); Azure Defender compliance: Pass
ground_truth: GLBA Safeguards Rule requires institution to control encryption keys for systems storing financial information. Microsoft-managed keys mean Microsoft could theoretically access data. CMK is required but missing.
remediation_impact: GLBA non-compliance. Annual audit finding if not corrected. Requires migration to customer-managed keys in Azure Key Vault — 2-week project.

scenario: University hospital research team claimed their patient dataset was de-identified under HIPAA Safe Harbor and made the S3 bucket public for research sharing. CSPM shows no violation since public access for de-identified data appears acceptable. However, the dataset contains 17 geographic sub-divisions smaller than a state, violating Safe Harbor requirement that geographic data be limited to 3-digit ZIP codes or state level.
why_misclassified: EC-51 HIPAA Safe Harbor de-identification failure: scanner sees public bucket with data tagged as de-identified and passes. It cannot validate whether the de-identification method was properly applied. City-level geocoding in the dataset violates 45 CFR §164.514(b).
detection_signal: S3 bucket has public read; data tagged as deidentified=true; no PHI pattern matched by Macie at field level
ground_truth: Dataset contains city-level location data for patients in rare disease cohort (<20,000 people in some geographies). Re-identification risk is high. HIPAA Safe Harbor requires geographic units with >20,000 people or state-level only.
remediation_impact: HIPAA PHI breach — potentially 850 patient records. Required: immediate bucket lockdown, incident response, HHS breach notification within 60 days.

scenario: A suspicious CloudTrail log gap appears on a Sunday at 2am UTC but the CSPM does not alert because it compares the gap timestamp to the local university server time (US/Eastern, UTC-5). The CSPM's timezone logic calculates this as Saturday 9pm — a normal low-activity period — and suppresses the alert as expected low-volume.
why_misclassified: EC-48 timezone mismatch: CloudTrail timestamps are always UTC. CSPM baseline was calculated using local time. The apparent Saturday night gap actually represents a Sunday morning active business period in UTC+8 (APAC partner institution access window) during which 2,300 API calls were deleted.
detection_signal: CloudTrail gap detected at 2026-02-22T02:00:00Z; baseline shows low activity for Sat 9pm local; alert suppressed
ground_truth: 2,300 CloudTrail records deleted between 02:00-04:00 UTC Sunday. This aligns with scheduled access from APAC institutional partner. Log deletion is not expected from any automated process. Active investigation required.
remediation_impact: Potential evidence destruction or active attacker covering tracks. Incident response required. GLBA audit trail integrity compromised.

scenario: The transcript PDF generation Lambda runs on Python 3.8 (EOL). AWS Inspector shows no vulnerability findings because the function has no OS-level packages to scan — it's a pure Python function. The Python 3.8 runtime itself contains known security vulnerabilities post-EOL but Inspector's package-level scanner doesn't flag runtime EOL as a finding.
why_misclassified: EC-01 ghost package: the runtime vulnerability is not surfaced because it's in the managed Lambda execution environment layer, not the customer deployment package. Inspector scans the deployment package only.
detection_signal: No Inspector findings for this Lambda; runtime shows as python3.8
ground_truth: Python 3.8 reached EOL October 2024. AWS will stop security patches for python3.8 runtime. Function processes FERPA-protected student transcript data. Runtime-level CVEs not visible to package scanner.
remediation_impact: Silent EOL runtime risk. Function must be migrated to Python 3.12 before runtime retirement. Failure to act creates unpatched execution environment for FERPA-data processing.

scenario: GCP Artifact Analysis shows no critical vulnerabilities for the gradebook API image. The image SBOM was generated at build time and includes a vendored fork of a popular JWT library. The fork patched the original but introduced a new deserialization vulnerability that has no CVE assigned yet. The SBOM scanner only matches against known CVE databases.
why_misclassified: EC-44 SBOM unregistered vulnerability: the vendor fork contains a novel vulnerability not yet in any CVE database. SBOM scanning against CVE/NVD/OSV cannot detect vulnerabilities without a registered identifier. The fork's patch introduced the new flaw.
detection_signal: Artifact Analysis: 0 critical, 0 high CVEs; SBOM scan: pass
ground_truth: JWT library fork has deserialization flaw in token parsing path. Discovered by internal pen test. No CVE yet (reported to CERT 2 weeks ago). Scanner correctly reports no known CVEs — but the risk is real and actively exploitable.
remediation_impact: Gradebook API is publicly accessible. JWT deserialization flaw could allow authentication bypass for student grade records. FERPA breach risk.

scenario: Security Hub flags a VPC NACL for allowing all inbound traffic (0.0.0.0/0 on all ports). The NACL sits at the edge of the university's research collaboration zone. The actual access control is implemented at the security group layer for each instance, which have highly restrictive rules. The permissive NACL is intentional to allow stateless traffic from dynamic research partner IPs.
why_misclassified: EC-17 NACL lockdown: NACL is permissive but security groups provide the actual enforcement layer. Defense in depth recommends both, but the security group controls are present and effective. NACL=allow-all with SG=restrictive is a valid architecture pattern for dynamic-IP research environments.
detection_signal: NACL rule 100: allow all traffic from 0.0.0.0/0
ground_truth: All 12 instances in the subnet have security groups allowing only specific ports from specific CIDRs. SG evaluation occurs regardless of NACL. Permissive NACL + restrictive SG is a documented pattern for research computing.
remediation_impact: Tightening NACLs for dynamic research partner IPs requires maintaining an ever-changing NACL allow list, which is operationally impractical for a research collaboration network with 200+ partner institutions.

scenario: Security Hub flags an EC2 p3.8xlarge GPU instance as a potential zombie resource because it has been stopped for 3 months. The instance is the primary compute node for a summer research project that runs May-August. The instance is deliberately stopped from September through April to avoid compute costs.
why_misclassified: EC-11 sunset/lifecycle pattern: the instance follows an annual academic schedule. It was stopped on August 31 and is expected to restart May 1. Tags include schedule=summer-only. This is planned, not abandoned.
detection_signal: EC2 instance stopped for 92 days; no activity in 90-day window
ground_truth: Instance tagged: schedule=summer-only, project=nih-r01-ai123456, pi=prof.smith@university.edu. Stopping in September and restarting in May is the documented lifecycle. EBS volumes are encrypted and contain irreplaceable research data.
remediation_impact: Terminating the instance would destroy 400GB of irreplaceable genomics research data (NIH R01 grant, 3 years of computation). EBS volumes contain intermediate results that cannot be regenerated.

scenario: AWS Inspector flags CVE-2024-23897 (Jenkins arbitrary file read) as CRITICAL on a university CI/CD server running Jenkins 2.441. Investigation reveals the Jenkins CLI (which is the attack vector) is disabled via jenkins.CLI.disabled=true in the JVM startup arguments. The CVE requires CLI access to exploit.
why_misclassified: EC-04 dead code / disabled feature: Jenkins CLI is explicitly disabled at startup. The attack vector for CVE-2024-23897 requires CLI connection. With CLI disabled, the code path is unreachable regardless of the installed Jenkins version.
detection_signal: Jenkins 2.441 matched against CVE-2024-23897; CVSS 9.8 critical
ground_truth: JVM arg: -Djenkins.CLI.disabled=true confirmed in /etc/default/jenkins. Verified: curl http://jenkins:8080/cli returns 404. CLI endpoint not served. CVE attack vector is absent.
remediation_impact: Upgrading Jenkins version is good practice but provides no immediate security improvement given CLI is disabled. Upgrade should follow normal change management, not emergency patching.

scenario: AWS Inspector flags CVE-2024-2961 (glibc iconv buffer overflow) in the LMS web application container. The vulnerability exists in glibc's iconv() function when used with specific charset conversions. The application uses Python's built-in codec module which bypasses glibc's iconv entirely.
why_misclassified: EC-02 build layer: glibc is present in the container image but the application's charset conversion path uses Python's internal codec, not glibc's iconv(). The vulnerable code path in glibc is not reached by any application call.
detection_signal: glibc 2.35 detected in container; CVE-2024-2961 matched by version
ground_truth: Application code: import codecs — uses Python built-in, not ctypes or cffi. strace confirms no iconv_open() syscalls during normal operation. glibc package present but iconv code path unreachable.
remediation_impact: Patching glibc addresses the finding but provides no actual security improvement for this application. Creates unnecessary deployment risk mid-semester.

scenario: GCP SCC flags a HIGH CVE in the Envoy proxy sidecar container in the Canvas LMS pod. The CVE is in Envoy's gRPC implementation. The Canvas LMS service mesh uses mTLS with Istio but does not use gRPC — all inter-service communication is HTTP/1.1 REST. The vulnerable gRPC code path is compiled in but never invoked.
why_misclassified: EC-32 sidecar proxy CVE with strict mTLS: the gRPC vulnerability in Envoy is unreachable because the mesh configuration uses HTTP/1.1 only (http_protocol_options) with gRPC disabled at the listener level.
detection_signal: Envoy proxy 1.28.1 container; CVE matched by version; severity HIGH
ground_truth: Istio VirtualService uses httpRoute only. Envoy filter chain has no grpc_http1_bridge filter. gRPC feature flag disabled. Confirmed via istioctl proxy-config listeners — no gRPC port listeners.
remediation_impact: Patching Envoy requires rolling restart of all LMS pods during class hours, risking disruption to active student sessions for a vulnerability with no reachable attack path.

scenario: GCP SCC flags the LTI grade callback Cloud Run service for having public ingress enabled. The service receives grade passback callbacks from external LTI tools (Turnitin, Gradescope, Respondus) and must be internet-accessible by design. An org policy was created to block public Cloud Run services but was explicitly overridden for this service via a resource-level policy.
why_misclassified: EC-40 GCP Cloud Run org policy override: the org policy AllowedIngressSettings was overridden at the resource level for this specific service. The override is documented in the architecture decision record. Public access is the LTI standard requirement.
detection_signal: Cloud Run service ingress=all; org policy AllowedIngressSettings=internal-and-cloud-load-balancing violated
ground_truth: Resource-level override is intentional and approved. Service validates HMAC signatures on all callbacks (LTI 1.3 signed requests). Only authenticated POST requests from known LTI tool client IDs are processed. Override documented in ADR-2024-047.
remediation_impact: Removing public ingress breaks LTI grade passback from Turnitin and Gradescope for all courses using plagiarism detection and automated grading.

scenario: ECR image scanning flags a CRITICAL CVE in the exam proctoring service container. The image is built on gcr.io/distroless/python3. The CVE is in bash (not present in distroless). The scanner matched the CVE against the base image's OS label without validating that bash is actually installed.
why_misclassified: EC-29 distroless image CVE: distroless images intentionally exclude shell utilities. The CVE requires bash to be present. Distroless has no /bin/bash, /bin/sh, or any shell. The attack vector (AV:L requires local shell) is inaccessible.
detection_signal: ECR scan matched bash CVE against python3-distroless:latest; CVSS 7.2
ground_truth: docker run --rm proctoring-service:latest which bash returns exit code 1 — bash not found. Distroless explicitly removes all shells. Attack vector AV:L requires shell to be exploitable. Finding is a scanner false positive.
remediation_impact: No action required. Scanner should detect distroless images and suppress shell CVEs automatically.

scenario: ECR scanning flags a HIGH CVE in the database migration CronJob image. This image runs schema migrations via kubectl apply jobs on a monthly basis — runs for approximately 45 seconds and then terminates. The CVE requires a persistent network connection to exploit over time.
why_misclassified: EC-33 ephemeral CronJob pod: the container exists for ~45 seconds per run. The CVE requires establishing a persistent connection (exploit window > 60 seconds). The pod terminates before any realistic exploit chain can complete.
detection_signal: Container image has HIGH CVE; image runs as CronJob in production namespace
ground_truth: CronJob schedule: 0 2 1 * * (first of month, 2am). Pod lifespan: 40-50 seconds. CVE requires TCP connection establishment + 3 round trips minimum. Temporal attack window is insufficient for exploitation.
remediation_impact: Patching the migration job image is good hygiene but carries near-zero active risk due to ephemeral nature. Schedule for next planned maintenance window.

scenario: AWS Inspector flags a CVE in the OpenSSL library for the enrollment sync Lambda. The CVE is in the Lambda managed runtime layer (provided by AWS), not in the customer deployment package. The customer code uses boto3 which uses the runtime's OpenSSL. AWS has already patched this in the managed runtime but the scanner reports the customer as the owner.
why_misclassified: EC-36 Lambda managed runtime vs customer code: the vulnerable package is in the AWS-managed layer, not the customer deployment. Remediation ownership belongs to AWS for managed runtime packages, not the customer. AWS patches these automatically.
detection_signal: Inspector finding: OpenSSL CVE in Lambda function course-enrollment-sync; remediation owner assigned to customer
ground_truth: Package is in /opt/python/lib/python3.12/ (AWS managed layer path). Customer deployment at /var/task/ has no OpenSSL. AWS confirmed in Shield advisory that managed runtime layer was patched 3 days after CVE disclosure.
remediation_impact: Customer cannot patch managed runtime packages. Correct action: verify AWS has patched the runtime (confirmed) and close finding. No customer action required.

scenario: Security Hub flags the lecture video transcription output bucket for lacking customer-managed key (CMK) encryption. The bucket uses S3-SSE (AES-256 with AWS-managed keys), which does provide encryption at rest. The finding is triggered by a custom rule requiring CMK for all buckets containing student data, but the SSE provides actual encryption — just not with customer-controlled keys.
why_misclassified: EC-39 serverless no encryption = missing CMK not missing encryption: S3-SSE with AWS-managed keys is real encryption. The finding description says 'no encryption' but the actual gap is the key management model, not the absence of encryption. Misleading severity assigned.
detection_signal: Custom rule: CMK required for student-data buckets; bucket uses SSE-S3 not SSE-KMS
ground_truth: Bucket IS encrypted with S3-SSE (AES-256). Data at rest is protected. The compliance gap is specifically key custody — CMK would give the university control over key rotation and revocation. This is a compliance gap, not a security gap.
remediation_impact: CMK migration is a compliance project (GLBA Safeguards alignment), not an emergency. Data is not exposed. Timeline: 60-day migration plan rather than emergency patch.

scenario: A scholarship application Lambda uses a vendored fork of a popular form validation library. The university forked it 2 years ago to add custom FERPA data handling. The fork was not maintained and diverged significantly from upstream. A dependency confusion attack planted a malicious version of the upstream package on PyPI that matches the fork's import namespace. Scanner shows no findings because package hash matches the vendored copy — not the malicious PyPI version. But the PyPI version would be pulled on fresh deploys.
why_misclassified: EC-42 vendored patched fork: scanner checks installed package against known CVE databases. The fork has no CVE because it's a private fork. The dependency confusion risk (malicious package on PyPI with same name) is invisible to vulnerability scanners.
detection_signal: Installed package hash matches internal vendored copy; no CVE matches in NVD/OSV/GHSA
ground_truth: Malicious package 'university-forms-validator' published to PyPI 3 weeks ago. Fresh CI builds without vendored cache would pull the malicious version. Existing deployments use cached vendored copy — currently safe but next deployment is at risk.
remediation_impact: Next deployment of scholarship processor would install malicious package. Financial aid PII (SSN, tax records) would be exfiltrated. Requires: namespace claim on PyPI, pin to vendored hash, deploy frozen requirements.

scenario: Azure Defender shows the student portal App Service as compliant for TLS. The App Service has MinTlsVersion=1.2. However, a feature flag in the application code ('legacy_browser_support') enables a TLS 1.0 compatibility mode via a custom middleware when set to true. This flag is currently true in the production app settings, allowing TLS 1.0 connections despite the platform setting.
why_misclassified: EC-45 feature flag disabled dep: the platform-level TLS enforcement says 1.2+ but an application-level feature flag re-enables TLS 1.0 via middleware. Scanner checks infrastructure configuration, not application feature flags.
detection_signal: Azure App Service MinTlsVersion=1.2; Azure Defender compliance: Pass
ground_truth: APPINSIGHTS_INSTRUMENTATIONKEY reveals APP_SETTINGS: FEATURE_LEGACY_BROWSER_SUPPORT=true. Application middleware enables TLS 1.0 handshakes for the /api/legacy/ endpoint path. Real-world TLS scan confirms TLSv1.0 accepted.
remediation_impact: TLS 1.0 vulnerability on FERPA/GLBA-scoped student portal. PCI-DSS 4.0 requires TLS 1.2 minimum. Set FEATURE_LEGACY_BROWSER_SUPPORT=false and redeploy.

scenario: GCP SCC shows no RBAC violations on the research Kubernetes cluster. The cluster has OPA Gatekeeper as an admission controller with policies restricting privileged containers. However, the ConstraintTemplate CRDs were deployed with a dry-run annotation (enforcement-action: dryRun) during initial testing and were never changed to 'deny'. All constraint violations are logged but never blocked.
why_misclassified: EC-31 admission controller compensating for RBAC: the CSPM sees OPA Gatekeeper is present and marks RBAC controls as compensated. It does not validate whether the Gatekeeper policies are in enforce vs. dry-run mode.
detection_signal: OPA Gatekeeper present in cluster; admission webhook registered; SCC marks as compliant
ground_truth: kubectl get constraints -o json | jq '.items[].spec.enforcementAction' returns 'dryRun' for all 8 constraint templates. No violations are blocked — only logged. Privileged container deployment is currently unblocked.
remediation_impact: Research cluster is running with OPA admission controller in audit-only mode. Privileged containers can be deployed by any namespace user. Change enforcementAction from dryRun to deny after validating no legitimate privileged workloads are running.

scenario: Security Hub identifies the student services web application standby instance as unused (0% CPU, no inbound connections for 14 days). The instance is the standby half of a blue-green deployment pair. It is intentionally idle and will receive traffic during the next deployment when the current active instance is decommissioned.
why_misclassified: EC-12 blue-green inactive: zero-traffic standby instances are a planned part of deployment architecture. The instance is healthy and ready to serve traffic on demand, not abandoned.
detection_signal: EC2 instance with 0% CPU utilization for 14 days; tagged prod; no CloudWatch alarms triggered
ground_truth: Instance tagged: deployment-role=standby, deployment-color=blue. ALB target group weight: 0% (standby). Last deployment rotation: 11 days ago. Instance will be active after next deployment cycle.
remediation_impact: Terminating the standby instance would break the blue-green deployment strategy and make zero-downtime deployments impossible for the student services portal.

scenario: GuardDuty flags anomalous S3 API activity from the financial aid disbursement service on January 1. The service makes 10x the normal number of S3 API calls. This is the start of the spring semester when all financial aid award letters are generated and emailed to returning students — a predictable annual spike.
why_misclassified: EC-23 warm-up/predictable spike window: GuardDuty's baseline was calculated excluding holiday periods and does not account for semester-start patterns. The January 1 spike is a known annual event, not anomalous activity.
detection_signal: S3:GetObject call volume 1,247% above 30-day baseline; GuardDuty medium finding escalated to HIGH
ground_truth: January 1 = spring semester start. Financial aid award letter generation runs 6am-2pm UTC on this date annually. Identical pattern documented in GuardDuty findings from Jan 1, 2023 and Jan 1, 2024 — both closed as FP.
remediation_impact: No action required. GuardDuty finding should be suppressed with a rule for semester-start dates. Recurring false alert wastes security analyst time (est. 2 hrs/year investigation).

scenario: Security Hub recommends creating VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB for the research collaboration VPC to prevent traffic from traversing the internet. The VPC has an S3 VPC endpoint policy that explicitly denies all buckets except the internal research data bucket. All other S3 traffic goes through the NAT gateway — which is the intended design for accessing external collaboration storage (e.g., AWS Open Data Registry, collaborator bucket).
why_misclassified: EC-18 VPC endpoint deny: the endpoint exists but with a restrict-all policy for external buckets, intentionally routing external S3 access through NAT. The finding misinterprets the intentional routing design as a missing endpoint.
detection_signal: S3 traffic for some buckets detected traversing NAT gateway; recommendation to use VPC endpoint for all S3
ground_truth: VPC endpoint policy: Allow s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::internal-research-data only. External S3 (NSF Open Data, NIH dbGaP) intentionally routed via NAT to reach internet-hosted collaborative resources.
remediation_impact: Routing all S3 through a restrictive VPC endpoint would block access to public research datasets on AWS Open Data Registry, breaking NIH-funded data access workflows.

scenario: GCP SCC reports a MEDIUM finding for the identity provisioning server having the default service account with broad permissions. In the normalized cross-cloud view, MEDIUM from GCP SCC maps to MEDIUM in the dashboard. However, GCP SCC's severity scale assigns MEDIUM to findings that AWS Security Hub would rate HIGH. The finding involves the default compute service account having project-level Editor role.
why_misclassified: EC-47 CSP severity scale non-equivalence: GCP SCC MEDIUM for an Editor-role default service account is equivalent to AWS HIGH for the same misconfiguration. Cross-cloud normalization is missing, causing the finding to be under-prioritized.
detection_signal: GCP SCC severity: MEDIUM; default compute SA has roles/editor; identity provisioning server
ground_truth: Default compute SA with roles/editor on identity provisioning server means the server can create/modify all GCP resources including IAM policies. This is a lateral movement vector. Normalized severity: HIGH. The GCP SCC MEDIUM label does not reflect the actual blast radius.
remediation_impact: Identity provisioning server compromise = full project takeover. Remove roles/editor from default SA and bind only required roles (roles/iam.serviceAccountUser scoped to specific resources).

scenario: Azure Defender flags the Blackboard LMS integration API for having a TLS certificate expiring in 7 days. The certificate shown is an internal health-check certificate on port 8443. The actual student-facing endpoint on port 443 uses App Service Managed Certificate with auto-renewal configured. Azure Defender is inspecting the wrong certificate.
why_misclassified: EC-41 Azure managed TLS termination: the expiring cert is for an internal health endpoint not exposed externally. The public-facing TLS is managed by Azure App Service with auto-renewal. The scanner found the wrong certificate.
detection_signal: Certificate expiry: 7 days; port 8443; App Service: blackboard-integration-api
ground_truth: Port 443: Azure App Service Managed Certificate, auto-renewal enabled, valid 87 days. Port 8443: internal health check, self-signed, intentionally short-lived, renewed automatically by health check deployment script every 30 days.
remediation_impact: No action required for security. Internal health check cert is expected to be short-lived. App Service managed cert is valid and auto-renewing.

scenario: GuardDuty detects an IAM credential exfiltration attempt (UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS) but the finding is auto-suppressed by a custom filter that suppresses all GuardDuty findings for the IP range 192.168.0.0/16 because it was previously used as a VPN range. The university changed VPN vendors 6 months ago — this range is no longer internal.
why_misclassified: EC-50 stale suppression filter: the GuardDuty suppression filter was created when the VPN used RFC-1918 space that appeared as internal. After VPN vendor change, the IP range became irrelevant but the suppression filter was never updated. Active credential theft is being silenced.
detection_signal: GuardDuty finding auto-suppressed by filter: source-ip-matches-internal-vpn-range
ground_truth: 192.168.88.45 is an attacker IP, not internal VPN. New VPN uses 172.16.0.0/12 range. GuardDuty finding represents real credential exfiltration from EC2 instance metadata. IAM credentials from financial aid processing role being used from external IP.
remediation_impact: Active security incident. Financial aid IAM credentials potentially compromised. Immediate: revoke and rotate credentials, block the source IP, investigate the EC2 instance for compromise.

scenario: Security Hub custom control flags the student auth service ECR repository for not enforcing image signing at the registry level. The university uses AWS Signer with Notation and has EKS admission webhook that validates signatures before pod scheduling. The scanner checks registry-level enforcement, missing the webhook-level enforcement.
why_misclassified: EC-35 image signing with admission enforcement: image signing IS enforced, just at the admission controller layer (EKS webhook) rather than at the registry pull layer. Scanner checks only ECR repository policy, not Kubernetes admission webhooks.
detection_signal: ECR repository has no image tag immutability; no AWS Signer policy at registry level
ground_truth: EKS has Notation admission webhook validating all pod images against university signing key before scheduling. kubectl describe validatingwebhookconfiguration notation-validator confirms all namespaces are covered. Unsigned images are rejected at deploy time.
remediation_impact: Adding ECR registry-level signing policy is defense-in-depth improvement but the actual control is already present and working at the admission controller. Medium priority hygiene item.

scenario: A developer accidentally set a public-read ACL on a specific S3 object (not the bucket) containing a Social Security Number export for FAFSA processing. The CSPM scans bucket-level ACLs and Block Public Access settings — the bucket itself has public access blocked. Object-level ACLs are not scanned. The file has been publicly accessible for 3 weeks.
why_misclassified: EC-45 scanner gap: CSPM checks bucket-level access controls but does not enumerate individual object ACLs. Object-level ACL can grant public access even when bucket-level BPA appears secure — this is a known scanner blind spot.
detection_signal: Bucket Block Public Access: Enabled; no bucket-level public ACL; no CSPM finding generated
ground_truth: Object ACL: public-read set on enrollment-exports/spring2025-ssn-extract.csv. File contains 8,200 SSNs for FAFSA. Object has been indexed by at least one web crawler based on access logs. Block Public Access at bucket level does NOT override existing object ACLs when set after the fact.
remediation_impact: Active FERPA and GLBA breach. 8,200 SSNs exposed. Required: immediately revoke object ACL, notify affected students, file breach report with Department of Education and FTC.

scenario: Security Hub shows a HIGH finding for an EC2 instance missing security patches. The instance was terminated 45 days ago but Security Hub continues to show the finding as ACTIVE because finding auto-archival only triggers after 90 days of no updates for terminated resources. The dashboard shows inflated open finding count.
why_misclassified: EC-24 stale scan: finding refers to a resource that no longer exists. The instance was terminated as part of a LMS platform migration. Security Hub has not yet archived the orphaned finding.
detection_signal: SecurityHub finding ACTIVE; EC2 instance i-0old-lms-instance; HIGH severity missing patches
ground_truth: aws ec2 describe-instances --instance-ids i-0old-lms-instance returns empty Reservations[]. Instance terminated 2025-12-15. Finding is an artifact of Security Hub's 90-day archive delay for terminated resource findings.
remediation_impact: Finding should be manually archived. No security action required. Inflates open finding count causing prioritization noise.

scenario: CIS control flags an ALB serving OpenCourseWare static assets for having access logging disabled. The ALB serves only publicly cached static files (CSS, JS, images). All meaningful access logs are captured at the CloudFront distribution layer upstream with full request metadata. ALB logging was disabled to avoid duplicate log storage costs.
why_misclassified: EC-05 WAF/CDN-shielded: CloudFront captures all request data including client IPs, user agents, and cache hit/miss before traffic reaches the ALB. ALB access logs would be redundant. The forensic record exists at the CDN layer.
detection_signal: ALB access_logs.s3.enabled=false; CIS 3.x logging control failed
ground_truth: CloudFront distribution cf-0abc123 has access logging enabled to s3://ocw-cdn-logs/. Log fields include x-forwarded-for, cs-uri-stem, sc-status, and time-taken. ALB only sees forwarded traffic after CDN processing.
remediation_impact: Enabling ALB logs creates duplicate data at $0.008/GB, estimated $180/month additional cost. No security improvement as CloudFront logs provide equivalent coverage.

scenario: ECR scanning flags a HIGH CVE in the course import container image for a vulnerable version of Python's urllib3. The CVE only exists in an init container that validates configuration files at pod startup and exits before any student data flows. The main application container uses a patched version of urllib3.
why_misclassified: EC-30 init container CVE: the vulnerable package is in the init container which runs to completion before the pod becomes READY. The init container never handles student data or network traffic during steady-state operation. It runs once per pod start and exits with code 0.
detection_signal: Container image course-importer-init:v1.2.0 contains urllib3 1.26.18; CVE matched
ground_truth: Init container runs config validation only: reads ConfigMap, validates schema, exits. No network requests, no data processing. Main app container (course-importer:v1.2.0) uses urllib3 2.0.7 (patched). The vuln cannot be reached during normal operations.
remediation_impact: Updating init container image is correct hygiene but carries near-zero actual risk. Schedule for next planned deployment cycle.

scenario: Security Hub flags a development security group for having a broad CIDR range on port 3000. The security group is in a faculty development sandbox account used exclusively for web development courses. Students run local React dev servers on port 3000 for peer code review. No production data, no PII, no cross-account access from this environment.
why_misclassified: EC-09 dev inflation: applying production-level network controls to a development sandbox ignores the context. The sandbox was provisioned with intentionally relaxed rules for pedagogical purposes. No student PII is accessible from or within this environment.
detection_signal: Security group allows TCP/3000 from 0.0.0.0/0; environment tag: dev; severity inflated to HIGH
ground_truth: Account has no IAM roles with cross-account trust. No S3 buckets with real data. No RDS instances. Used exclusively for CS 302 (Web Development) coursework. Environment tag dev confirmed in account metadata.
remediation_impact: Restricting dev sandbox network rules would break peer code review workflow for 35 students in the web development course.

scenario: AWS Inspector shows no vulnerabilities for the student records API Lambda. The function has a requirements.txt with cryptography==41.0.0 listed as a test dependency. During Docker-based local testing, cryptography 41.0.0 is used. But the Lambda deployment uses a Lambda Layer that pins to cryptography==38.0.4, which has CVE-2023-49083 (NULL pointer dereference). The Layer version is stale and not scanned by Inspector.
why_misclassified: EC-43 build-time vs runtime: Inspector scans the deployment package requirements.txt which shows 41.0.0. The actual runtime uses a Lambda Layer that pins 38.0.4. Inspector doesn't scan Layer content separately from the function package.
detection_signal: Inspector scans function deployment zip: requirements.txt shows cryptography==41.0.0; no finding generated
ground_truth: Lambda Layer arn:aws:lambda:us-east-1:900112233445:layer:student-api-deps:7 contains cryptography 38.0.4. Runtime import path resolves Layer before function package. CVE-2023-49083 is present in the actual execution environment.
remediation_impact: Student records API processes FERPA-protected data. Cryptography library vulnerability in actual runtime. Update Lambda Layer to cryptography>=41.0.0.

scenario: Security Hub flags the quiz session token DynamoDB table for not having point-in-time recovery enabled. The table stores short-lived JWT session tokens for active quiz sessions with a 1-hour TTL. All items expire within 60 minutes. There is no meaningful data to recover — the table is essentially a cache of ephemeral auth tokens.
why_misclassified: EC-22 tokenization/ephemeral store: PITR for a session token cache provides no business value. Tokens expire in 60 minutes. Recovering a 3-day-old state would mean recovering expired, already-invalidated session tokens with zero utility.
detection_signal: DynamoDB table PointInTimeRecovery.Enabled=false; table tagged as student-data
ground_truth: Table contains only: session_id (UUID), expiry_timestamp (epoch+3600), user_id (hashed). All items have TTL. Table recoverable from scratch in seconds as it's purely derived from active sessions. student-data tag inherited from account-level tagging policy, not semantically accurate.
remediation_impact: Enabling PITR adds ~$0.20/GB/month for a table that holds ephemeral tokens. No recovery scenario exists where restoring this table has value.

scenario: An IAM Access Analyzer finding for an overpermissive EdTech vendor integration role was suppressed 18 months ago with the rationale 'vendor requires broad access per contract.' The vendor contract was renegotiated 8 months ago and the scope of access was reduced, but no one updated the IAM policy or removed the suppression. The role still has s3:* and dynamodb:* on all resources.
why_misclassified: EC-49 stale suppression with changed context: the suppression was valid at the time but the underlying justification changed. The new vendor contract specifies read-only access to specific buckets only. The broad permissions are now out of contract scope.
detection_signal: IAM Access Analyzer finding suppressed with reason: vendor-contract-requirement (suppressed 2024-08-15)
ground_truth: Vendor contract v2 (signed 2025-06-01) specifies: s3:GetObject on arn:aws:s3:::edtech-lms-data only. Current role has s3:* and dynamodb:* on *. Vendor has write access to student data they no longer contractually need.
remediation_impact: EdTech vendor has unauthorized write access to student learning data (FERPA-protected). Scope role to match new contract terms immediately. Risk of data misuse or breach by vendor.

scenario: GCP SCC flags a firewall rule allowing HTTP (port 80) from all sources on the K-12 school district's content filtering proxy. CIPA requires content filtering for schools receiving E-rate funding. The proxy must accept HTTP traffic from student devices to intercept and filter before forwarding. HTTPS traffic is handled via SSL inspection.
why_misclassified: EC-06 CIDR-gated: the HTTP endpoint is the student-facing ingress for content filtering — a CIPA compliance requirement. All traffic passes through inspection. The apparent open port is the compliance control, not a vulnerability.
detection_signal: Firewall rule allows TCP/80 from 0.0.0.0/0; K-12 environment with COPPA/CIPA scope
ground_truth: Content filtering proxy intercepts all HTTP traffic from student subnets (10.100.0.0/16). Port 80 must be reachable for pre-authentication redirect flows. CIPA E-rate compliance auditor approved this architecture in 2024.
remediation_impact: Blocking port 80 would break HTTP content filtering, violating CIPA requirements and risking loss of E-rate funding ($2.1M/year).

scenario: GCP SCC flags a public GCS bucket containing the university's HathiTrust digitized book archive mirror. The bucket contains 2.3 million public domain book scans served to the global academic community. The content is explicitly out-of-copyright and mirrored per HathiTrust data sharing agreement requiring public availability.
why_misclassified: EC-20 empty vault/public content: the bucket contains only public domain scanned texts. No student data, no PII, no FERPA-scoped content. Public access is contractually required by the HathiTrust data partnership agreement.
detection_signal: GCS bucket allUsers have roles/storage.objectViewer; bucket tagged: contains_pii=inherited
ground_truth: All 2.3M objects are scanned public domain books (pre-1928 publication dates). HathiTrust partnership contract clause 4.2 requires public read access. FERPA does not apply to historical library collections.
remediation_impact: Restricting access would violate the HathiTrust partnership agreement and remove access for 50,000+ researchers globally who use this archive.

scenario: AWS Security Hub shows no EKS RBAC violations. The cluster has a ClusterRoleBinding that grants system:masters to a group called 'eks-admin'. The binding was created during initial cluster setup. The group membership is managed via AWS IAM identity mapping. A recently onboarded developer's IAM user was mistakenly added to the 'eks-admin' IAM group, giving them unrestricted cluster access without security team awareness.
why_misclassified: EC-31 admission controller gap: Security Hub checks for known bad configurations at the cluster level but doesn't evaluate who is currently in the eks-admin IAM group. The RBAC binding itself looks valid; the overpermissive membership is in IAM, not in Kubernetes.
detection_signal: EKS RBAC: ClusterRoleBinding eks-admin exists; maps to IAM group; no Security Hub finding
ground_truth: IAM group 'eks-admin' has 8 members. Developer jsmith@university.edu was added by mistake 3 weeks ago. jsmith has no legitimate need for cluster admin. The IAM → K8s trust path gives jsmith kubectl access with system:masters rights on the student services cluster.
remediation_impact: Developer with cluster admin access on FERPA-data cluster is an insider threat risk. Remove from eks-admin IAM group. Implement least-privilege namespace-scoped bindings.

scenario: Azure Defender flags the Banner SIS Azure SQL database for having Azure SQL Auditing disabled. The university uses a third-party database activity monitoring (DAM) tool (Imperva SecureSphere) deployed as a network-level appliance that captures all SQL traffic at the network layer. Azure SQL Auditing is redundant and was intentionally disabled to avoid duplicate log costs.
why_misclassified: EC-13 app-layer compensating control: a dedicated DAM solution captures all database activity at the network layer. Azure SQL's built-in auditing would be a duplicate log stream. The actual audit requirement is met by Imperva with richer detail than Azure SQL native auditing.
detection_signal: Azure SQL Auditing State=Disabled; database tagged: ferpa-scoped=true
ground_truth: Imperva SecureSphere DAM monitors all SQL connections on TCP/1433. Captures: full query text, query parameters, client IP, user, session metadata. Logs shipped to Splunk with 1-year retention. FERPA audit requirement is satisfied.
remediation_impact: Enabling Azure SQL auditing creates duplicate logs at ~$400/month additional cost. No compliance gap exists given Imperva coverage.

scenario: Security Hub flags the LMS session cache Redis cluster for not having an AUTH token configured. The cluster is deployed in an isolated VPC with no internet gateway. It's accessible only from the LMS application servers via security group rules allowing only port 6379 from the app tier SG. Network-level isolation is the primary access control.
why_misclassified: EC-08 VPC-bounded: the Redis cluster is in a private subnet with no external access path. Security group restrictions limit access to only the application tier. AUTH token adds marginal security in an already-isolated network segment.
detection_signal: ElastiCache cluster authTokenEnabled=false; FERPA-scoped data in session store
ground_truth: VPC has no IGW. Redis SG allows TCP/6379 only from sg-0app-tier. No peered VPCs with external access. All application hosts are managed EC2 instances. Network isolation provides equivalent protection to AUTH token in this topology.
remediation_impact: Adding AUTH token is security improvement but non-urgent given network isolation. Should be in next maintenance window, not emergency change.

scenario: The student transcript primary bucket has cross-region replication to us-west-2. An attacker modified the replication configuration to add a third destination bucket in an attacker-controlled account. S3 replication config changes are logged in CloudTrail but the CSPM only checks for 'replication enabled' (compliant) not 'replication destinations are authorized' (misconfigured).
why_misclassified: EC-48 scanner checks existence not correctness: CSPM validates that replication is configured (correct) but doesn't validate that all replication destinations are within authorized accounts. The malicious third destination is in a different AWS account.
detection_signal: S3 bucket replication: enabled; CSPM check: pass (replication is enabled)
ground_truth: Replication config has 2 rules: rule-1 → us-west-2 (university DR account 445566778899), rule-2 → ap-east-1 (unknown account 999111222333). Rule-2 was added 9 days ago via compromised AWS credential. All new transcripts being exfiltrated to attacker bucket.
remediation_impact: Active data exfiltration. FERPA transcript data being copied to attacker account. Immediate: remove unauthorized replication rule, rotate credentials, investigate how rule was added, notify affected students.

scenario: GCP SCC flags a service account as unused because it has had no activity in 90 days. The account is used for annual genomics batch processing that runs once per year (January). The account was last active January 15 and will be active again next January. It follows a known annual research processing cycle.
why_misclassified: EC-26 headless SA with annual schedule: SA inactivity is expected and intentional. The service account is attached to a Pub/Sub subscription that triggers only when the annual batch job is submitted. 90-day inactivity threshold is appropriate for most accounts but not for annual batch processing.
detection_signal: Service account last activity: 90+ days; GCP SCC recommendation: delete or disable
ground_truth: SA tagged: schedule=annual, next_use=2027-01, pi=dr.jones@university.edu, grant=nih-r35-gm123456. Account is dormant by design between January processing runs. Disabling would prevent NIH-funded annual genomics pipeline from running.
remediation_impact: Disabling or deleting the SA would break the NIH-funded annual batch pipeline. Researcher would need to recreate SA and update all pipeline configurations before next January run.

scenario: Security Hub flags a security group that allows all traffic between members of the same SG (self-referencing rule). This security group covers the 200+ nodes of an HPC cluster where MPI (Message Passing Interface) jobs require any-to-any communication between nodes on dynamic ports. Restricting this would break all parallel computing jobs.
why_misclassified: EC-17 NACL/SG pattern for HPC: MPI-based HPC jobs require unrestricted intra-cluster communication. The self-referencing SG rule limits traffic to the HPC cluster subnet members only — external traffic is blocked. This is the standard AWS ParallelCluster networking pattern.
detection_signal: Security group has rule: allow all traffic from sg-0hpc-cluster-internal (self); HIGH severity
ground_truth: Self-referencing SG rule allows only intra-cluster traffic. All 200 nodes are internal HPC compute nodes. No internet traffic. No student data flows through HPC compute nodes (only batch job code and outputs). AWS ParallelCluster documentation explicitly recommends this pattern.
remediation_impact: Restricting intra-cluster traffic would break MPI job communication and make the $2M HPC cluster unusable for all parallel computing research.

scenario: IAM Access Analyzer shows no findings for the FERPA audit report generator Lambda. The function's execution role was reviewed and approved 12 months ago with permissions scoped to read-only S3 and DynamoDB access. However, 2 months ago a developer added s3:PutObject to the role for a 'temporary' debug feature to write intermediate results. The temporary permission was never removed and Access Analyzer's last scan predates the change.
why_misclassified: EC-44 SBOM gap: Access Analyzer finding was closed after the original review. The permission addition was not flagged because there was no new finding generated — only an incremental policy change to an existing, previously-reviewed role.
detection_signal: IAM Access Analyzer: No active findings for role; last analyzed: 45 days ago
ground_truth: Role policy was modified 60 days ago to add s3:PutObject on arn:aws:s3:::ferpa-audit-reports/*. This gives the Lambda write access to FERPA audit records — a compliance violation (audit logs should be immutable). Change was made by dev without security review.
remediation_impact: Lambda can now overwrite or corrupt FERPA audit logs. Regulatory risk: FERPA audit trail integrity. Remove s3:PutObject from role and enable S3 Object Lock on audit bucket.

scenario: Amazon Macie flags the NLP research training corpus bucket for containing names, email addresses, and phone numbers. The bucket contains a 500GB scrape of publicly available academic paper metadata used to train a citation recommendation model. All data was sourced from public APIs (Semantic Scholar, arXiv). The personal information belongs to paper authors who have published their contact info publicly.
why_misclassified: EC-21 synthetic/public data: Macie correctly identifies PII patterns but cannot distinguish between privately collected PII and publicly available academic author contact information. The data was legally collected from public sources and is used for academic research.
detection_signal: Macie identifies: email addresses (45,000), phone numbers (2,300), names (890,000) in research corpus
ground_truth: All personal information is from public academic paper metadata. Authors voluntarily publish this information in academic papers. No student data, no enrollment records, no financial information. IRB protocol covers public data use.
remediation_impact: Restricting this bucket would halt NIH-funded NLP research project using publicly available academic metadata. No actual privacy violation exists.

scenario: Azure Defender flags a proctoring exam VM for missing OS patches. The VM was created 2 hours ago by auto-scaling for a final exam session and will be automatically deleted in 4 hours when the exam ends. The patch deployment pipeline hasn't run yet on this newly provisioned instance.
why_misclassified: EC-10 ephemeral workload: the VM lifespan (4 hours) is shorter than the patch deployment pipeline cadence (daily at midnight). The instance will be deleted before any exploitation is feasible. Patch findings on ephemeral instances create noise without security value.
detection_signal: VM missing 12 OS patches; Defender severity HIGH; VM age: 2 hours
ground_truth: VM provisioned by Terraform at exam start; scheduled termination script runs at exam end + 30 min. Average lifespan: 3.5 hours. OS patches would be applied by daily update job but VM terminates before job runs. New VMs are always provisioned from the latest approved base image.
remediation_impact: Creating exam VMs from pre-patched golden images is the correct fix (current project: quarterly image refresh). Per-instance patching of ephemeral VMs is operationally impractical.

scenario: AWS Inspector previously flagged CVE-2024-XXXX on the SIS application server. A vendor advisory stated the CVE was 'not applicable' to their product and the finding was suppressed. Six months later, a PoC exploit was published proving the CVE IS applicable to the vendor's deployment model. Inspector still shows the finding as suppressed.
why_misclassified: EC-46 reversed vendor dispute: the CVE was suppressed based on the vendor's initial dispute. The dispute was later overturned by the security community with PoC evidence. The suppression was never revisited after the dispute reversal.
detection_signal: Inspector finding suppressed: vendor-not-applicable (suppressed 2025-06-01); status: suppressed
ground_truth: PoC exploit published 2025-11-15 demonstrating the CVE is exploitable on this vendor's product configuration. NVD advisory updated to remove the disputed tag. CVE CVSS: 8.8 HIGH. SIS handles FERPA and GLBA data.
remediation_impact: FERPA/GLBA data at risk. Remove suppression, apply vendor patch now available, investigate whether exploitation has occurred in the 5-month window since PoC release.

scenario: Security Hub flags an S3 bucket with a cross-account bucket policy as a potential data exfiltration risk. The bucket is part of a Big Ten Academic Alliance research data sharing consortium. The bucket policy explicitly allows 12 partner university AWS accounts to read anonymized research datasets per the consortium data sharing agreement.
why_misclassified: EC-27 intra-org trust: while these are technically external accounts, they are part of a formal academic consortium with data sharing agreements, IRB protocols, and DUAs in place. The cross-account access is governed and intentional.
detection_signal: S3 bucket policy allows GetObject from 12 external AWS account IDs; no resource-based policy justification in CSPM
ground_truth: Bucket policy includes all 12 Big Ten partner university accounts explicitly by ID. Data Use Agreement covers all 12 institutions. Bucket contains only de-identified anonymized research data (IRB confirmed). No FERPA-protected student data.
remediation_impact: Removing cross-account access would withdraw the university from the Big Ten research consortium, breaking active NIH multi-site research grants worth $8.2M.

scenario: CIS Benchmark check for root account usage monitoring shows PASS because a CloudWatch alarm exists for root account console login. However, the alarm's SNS topic was silently abandoned — the email subscription bounced 8 months ago when the security mailbox was migrated to a new domain. Alarm fires but no notification is delivered.
