why_misclassified: EC-50 control exists but is non-functional: CSPM checks for the existence of the alarm and SNS topic (both present, both passing). It does not validate whether the SNS subscription is active and confirmed.
detection_signal: CIS 1.7: CloudWatch alarm for root account usage exists; SNS topic configured; check: PASS
ground_truth: SNS subscription status: PendingConfirmation (for old address) and 1 subscription with status: deleted (migration). Last alarm fire: 3 weeks ago (legitimate security team test) — zero notifications received. Root account activity would go undetected.
remediation_impact: Active monitoring gap for the most privileged AWS credential. Re-subscribe security team DL to SNS topic. Validate end-to-end alert delivery monthly.

scenario: GCP SCC flags a kernel CVE on GKE nodes in the research cluster. The CVE is a privilege escalation requiring a shell in the container (AV:L). All pods in the cluster use distroless or scratch base images. No pod in the cluster has a shell binary available, making container escape via this CVE impossible.
why_misclassified: EC-29 distroless + kernel CVE: while the kernel version is vulnerable, exploitation requires execution of a shell payload in a container. All containers in this cluster are distroless/scratch — no shell is available. The practical exploit path requires shell access that doesn't exist.
detection_signal: GKE node kernel version matches CVE; CVSS 7.8 HIGH; local privilege escalation
ground_truth: kubectl get pods -A -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.spec.containers[*].image}' — all images are gcr.io/distroless/* or scratch. GKE node upgrade is still best practice but practical risk is low without shell access in any workload.
remediation_impact: Node pool upgrade is the correct action during next maintenance window. Not an emergency given distroless workloads prevent the shell-based exploit chain.

scenario: Azure Defender generates a CREDENTIAL_DUMPING alert on the university Active Directory domain controller. The alert is auto-suppressed because it matches a suppression rule created for 'approved pentesting activity' from 3 years ago that was never removed after the pentest concluded. An active attacker is running Mimikatz.
why_misclassified: EC-49 pentest suppression never removed: suppression rule was valid for a 2-week pentest engagement in 2022. Rule was created with no expiration date. Three years later, real attacker activity matches the same pattern and is silently suppressed.
detection_signal: Azure Defender alert: Credential Dumping; suppression rule: approved-pentest-2022; status: suppressed
ground_truth: No pentest is currently authorized. Credential dumping is active attacker activity. Domain controller compromise = full AD forest takeover = access to all 45,000 student accounts, email, FERPA records, financial aid systems.
remediation_impact: Active incident. Domain controller compromise in progress. Isolate DC, rotate krbtgt account, force password reset for all privileged accounts, activate IR playbook.

scenario: IAM Access Analyzer flags the Turnitin integration role for trusting an external AWS account. Turnitin is a plagiarism detection service used by faculty. The role allows Turnitin's service account to read assignment submission metadata from an S3 bucket for grade correlation. The trust is to Turnitin's documented production AWS account ID with ExternalId condition.
why_misclassified: EC-14 documented third-party integration: the external account trust is to a known, contracted EdTech vendor. ExternalId condition prevents confused deputy. FERPA Business Associate Agreement is in place. This is standard SaaS integration architecture.
detection_signal: IAM role trusts external account; Access Analyzer: external access detected
ground_truth: Trusted account is Turnitin's production AWS account (documented in vendor portal). ExternalId: turnitin-university-12345 (university-specific). Role allows only s3:GetObject on submissions bucket. FERPA BAA signed 2024-08.
remediation_impact: Revoking Turnitin access would disable plagiarism detection for all 15,000 course submissions per semester, violating academic integrity policy.

scenario: GCP Artifact Analysis shows no critical vulnerabilities for the admission portal image. The image uses a multi-stage build where the build stage installs vulnerable packages. The final stage copies only the compiled binary. Artifact Analysis scans the final stage and sees only the clean binary — not the vulnerable build tools that ran during image creation.
why_misclassified: EC-43 multi-stage build blind spot: Artifact Analysis scans the final image layer only. Vulnerable packages in the build stage are excluded from the final image (correct) but if the build stage was compromised and injected malicious code into the binary, the scanner wouldn't detect it.
detection_signal: Artifact Analysis: final image scanned; 0 critical CVEs; all clear
ground_truth: The build pipeline uses a compromised base image for the build stage (supply chain attack). The malicious build stage inserted a reverse shell into the compiled admission portal binary during the latest build. Final image appears clean because the malicious code is in the compiled binary, not in package metadata.
remediation_impact: Admission portal serves 50,000 applicants including SSN and financial aid data. Reverse shell provides attacker code execution. Rebuild from trusted base image, rotate all secrets, investigate all builds in the last 30 days.

scenario: IAM Access Analyzer flags a role as unused for 90+ days. The role is used by the video streaming infrastructure for the university commencement ceremony — an annual event held in May. The role has been inactive since May and will be needed again next May for live streaming of graduation to families worldwide.
why_misclassified: EC-07 orphaned resource (false): the role appears orphaned but follows an annual usage cycle. Last used: May 2025 commencement. Next use: May 2026 commencement. Tags: schedule=annual, event=commencement.
detection_signal: IAM role last used: 8 months ago; IAM Access Analyzer: unused role recommendation
ground_truth: Role tagged: schedule=annual, event=graduation-ceremony, next_use=2026-05. Role allows MediaLive and S3 access for the graduation live stream. Used once per year during the 4-hour ceremony and rehearsal.
remediation_impact: Deleting this role would break the graduation ceremony live stream infrastructure, preventing families from watching commencement remotely.

scenario: CIS check for IAM password policy shows PASS. The policy requires 8-character minimum passwords with complexity. However, an IAM identity center (SSO) feature flag 'allow_legacy_console_access' is enabled for a set of department admin users, which bypasses SSO and allows direct IAM console login with the weaker legacy password policy instead of the SSO MFA requirement.
why_misclassified: EC-45 feature flag bypass: the password policy check passes at the account level. The feature flag creating a bypass path is in IAM Identity Center configuration — a separate service not scanned by the password policy check. The actual MFA requirement is bypassable.
detection_signal: IAM password policy: min length 8, complexity enabled; CIS check: PASS
ground_truth: IAM Identity Center setting AllowLegacyConsoleAccess=true for department admin groups. These users can authenticate directly to AWS console with IAM username/password, bypassing SSO MFA. 23 users affected. Minimum password length 8 is below NIST 800-63B recommendation of 12.
remediation_impact: Department admins can log in without MFA to FERPA/GLBA scoped AWS environment. Disable legacy console access flag in IAM Identity Center, enforce SSO for all human users.

scenario: GuardDuty flags unusual IAM activity from an IP in Romania. The university has a large international student body and a Romanian student enrolled in a summer online program is accessing the university's AWS-hosted student portal from their home country. The access pattern is flagged as unusual geography.
why_misclassified: EC-23 expected legitimate international access: the university serves students globally. Geography-based anomaly detection does not account for international student populations. The Romanian IP belongs to a residential ISP (not TOR/VPN/data center).
detection_signal: GuardDuty: UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/ConsoleLogin from Bucharest, Romania; deviation from baseline
ground_truth: User: student-20250712@university.edu. Login at 10:30 AM local time (Bucharest). IP belongs to RCS&RDS (major Romanian ISP). Student enrolled in CS Online Summer 2025, home address: Bucharest. Login is entirely expected.
remediation_impact: Blocking international access would prevent 3,200 international online students from accessing course materials and the student portal.

scenario: Security Hub compliance dashboard shows a high score (94%) for the university AWS environment. However, 17 Security Hub controls were disabled 2 years ago by a now-departed administrator to reduce alert noise. The disabled controls include IAM root MFA, CloudTrail encryption, and S3 public access blocking. The compliance percentage is calculated only over enabled controls.
why_misclassified: EC-50 inflated compliance score: Security Hub compliance percentage excludes disabled controls from the denominator. Disabling controls inflates the score without improving security. The 94% appears compliant but covers only the non-controversial controls.
detection_signal: Security Hub compliance: 94% PASSED; 17 controls disabled; dashboard shows green
ground_truth: 17 disabled controls include: IAM.6 (root MFA), CT.1 (CloudTrail encryption), S3.1 (S3 block public access). These are foundational controls. Re-enabling them would reveal an estimated 200+ active findings. True compliance: approximately 71%.
remediation_impact: Re-enable all 17 controls and remediate findings. The compliance score has been misleading leadership for 2 years. True security posture is significantly below reported metrics.

scenario: Security Hub flags the faculty research API ALB for not having a WAF associated. The ALB is internal-facing only (scheme=internal) and is accessible only from within the university VPC. All external traffic is handled by a CloudFront distribution with WAF attached that sits in front of the API.
why_misclassified: EC-16 edge-shielded: the WAF is at the CloudFront edge, not at the ALB. Internal ALBs behind CloudFront WAF do not require their own WAF — the edge protection filters malicious traffic before it reaches the internal ALB.
detection_signal: ALB has no associated WAF; ALB tagged as prod; FERPA data scope
ground_truth: ALB scheme=internal. CloudFront distribution cf-0def789 has WAF web ACL attached with OWASP rule group. All external requests go CloudFront → WAF → internal ALB. Direct access to internal ALB requires VPC membership (no internet path).
remediation_impact: Adding WAF to an internal-only ALB that is already protected by edge WAF provides no security improvement. Unnecessary cost (~$5/month per rule group).

scenario: CSPM flags the financial aid staging bucket with a LOW finding for S3 bucket versioning being disabled. The staging bucket was seeded with a copy of production data (unmasked SSNs, tax information) for a UI testing exercise 6 months ago. The staging environment received LOW severity treatment because of its environment tag, but it contains real production data.
why_misclassified: EC-47 CSP severity scale / environment context mismatch: the scanner correctly lowered severity for a 'staging' environment (MP-01 non-prod deflator). But this staging environment contains real, unmasked production FERPA/GLBA data — making the environment label inaccurate for risk purposes.
detection_signal: Staging bucket: S3 versioning disabled; environment=staging; severity downgraded to LOW
ground_truth: Bucket contains 8,500 real student financial aid records copied from production for manual UI testing. Contains: SSNs, AGI, tax transcript data. Bucket is internet-accessible (public read was never disabled). Environment tag 'staging' does not reflect the actual data sensitivity.
remediation_impact: Active GLBA/FERPA breach. Financial data exposed publicly. Immediate: revoke public access, delete production data from staging, notify affected students, file breach report.

scenario: IAM Access Analyzer flags the student portal application role for having cloudwatch:PutMetricData with resource=*. This is a standard CloudWatch Metrics permission that cannot be scoped to specific metric namespaces — AWS does not support resource-level restrictions for PutMetricData.
why_misclassified: EC-15 AWS service limitation: certain IAM actions do not support resource-level policies and must use wildcard resource. CloudWatch PutMetricData is one of them. The finding is technically correct but practically unavoidable — AWS documentation explicitly states resource-level permissions are not supported for this action.
detection_signal: IAM policy allows cloudwatch:PutMetricData on Resource: *; wildcard resource flagged
ground_truth: AWS IAM documentation: 'Resource-level permissions are not supported for cloudwatch:PutMetricData.' All compliant CloudWatch integrations must use resource: *. This is an AWS platform constraint, not a misconfiguration.
remediation_impact: Cannot be remediated — AWS platform does not support resource-level scoping for this action. Finding should be suppressed with justification: 'AWS service limitation for cloudwatch:PutMetricData.'

scenario: Security Hub flags the research data lake processed output bucket for not having S3 server access logging enabled. The bucket has no S3 access logging but all API calls (GetObject, PutObject, DeleteObject) are captured by CloudTrail data events, which provides equivalent or richer audit data than S3 access logging.
why_misclassified: EC-19 org-level logging: CloudTrail data events provide per-API-call logging for all S3 operations including requester identity, IP, and request parameters. S3 server access logging is a separate, less detailed mechanism. CSPM only checks S3 access logging flag, not CloudTrail data event coverage.
detection_signal: S3 bucket ServerAccessLogging.Enabled=false; FERPA-scoped bucket
ground_truth: CloudTrail has S3 data events enabled for this bucket (PutObject, GetObject, DeleteObject). Logs captured to s3://cloudtrail-logs-central/ with 7-year retention. CloudTrail provides: IAM identity, IP, request params, error codes — more detail than S3 access logs.
remediation_impact: Enabling S3 access logging creates duplicate log stream at additional cost with no audit coverage improvement. CloudTrail data events provide superior forensic coverage.

scenario: The student analytics dashboard ECR repository has scan-on-push enabled and shows 0 critical findings. The application uses a Python package from a private PyPI mirror that the university hosts internally. The internal mirror was compromised 3 weeks ago and a backdoored version of a statistics library was uploaded. ECR scan checks against public vulnerability databases and has no visibility into the internal mirror's integrity.
why_misclassified: EC-44 internal supply chain not scanned: ECR image scanning checks packages against NVD/OSV/Amazon Security Advisories. The backdoored package came from an internal mirror and has no CVE in public databases. The compromise is invisible to standard vulnerability scanning.
detection_signal: ECR scan: 0 critical, 0 high; repository has scan-on-push enabled; all clear
ground_truth: Internal PyPI mirror (pypi.university.edu) was compromised via weak admin password. Backdoored version of scikit-learn fork uploaded with data exfiltration capability. 15 applications installed the backdoored version over 3 weeks. No public CVE exists for this internal package.
remediation_impact: Student analytics data (grades, engagement metrics, FERPA-protected) being exfiltrated. Investigate internal PyPI mirror compromise, rebuild all affected images from clean packages, rotate credentials, assess data breach scope.

scenario: Azure Defender flags an Azure SQL database for missing recent patches. The database contains archived alumni records from 1990-2010 that were migrated to a read-only state 5 years ago. The database has no application tier pointing to it, is read-only, has no internet connectivity, and is maintained solely for legal hold requirements.
why_misclassified: EC-11 sunset lifecycle: this database is in a legal hold/archive state. It receives no writes, has no application users, and is inaccessible from the internet. Its sole purpose is meeting records retention requirements. Patch compliance risk is extremely low for a disconnected read-only archive.
detection_signal: Azure SQL missing patches; no recent backup; Defender recommendation: patch or retire
ground_truth: Database is read-only (ALTER DATABASE SET READ_ONLY). No connections in 2 years (verified in audit logs). VNET has no public endpoints. Maintained per university records retention policy (7 years post-last-enrollment). Legal hold lifted in 2027.
remediation_impact: Patching is appropriate but non-urgent. Database is isolated and read-only. Schedule for next maintenance window. Consider migration to cold storage (Azure Blob) to reduce SQL licensing cost.

scenario: A GCP SCC finding for an overpermissive IAM binding (allAuthenticatedUsers on a BigQuery dataset) was muted 14 months ago by a developer who thought it referred to a dev dataset. The actual resource is the financial aid BigQuery dataset containing GLBA-protected financial information. All Google-authenticated users (including any Google account holder) can query student financial data.
why_misclassified: EC-49 muted finding with incorrect justification: developer muted the finding believing it was a dev dataset. The SCC finding referenced the production financial aid dataset. Mute was applied without validating the resource path.
detection_signal: GCP SCC finding muted: allAuthenticatedUsers-iam-binding; muted by: dev-ops@university.edu; mute reason: dev-environment
ground_truth: BigQuery dataset: projects/university-finance/datasets/financial_aid_prod. IAM binding: allAuthenticatedUsers has roles/bigquery.dataViewer. Any Google account holder can query student financial aid data. Dataset contains 45,000 records with EFC, AGI, and award amounts.
remediation_impact: Active GLBA breach. Financial aid data queryable by anyone with a Google account. Immediately remove allAuthenticatedUsers binding, unmute the finding, investigate whether data was accessed.

scenario: Security Hub flags the LTI tool provider Lambda for having what appears to be a secret in an environment variable: 'LTI_CONSUMER_KEY=lms-platform-prod-key-2024'. The scanner's pattern matching identified 'key' in the variable name. The LTI consumer key is actually a non-secret identifier (not a password) used to identify the LMS platform in LTI protocol handshakes — it is paired with a separate shared secret stored in Secrets Manager.
why_misclassified: EC-04 dead code / semantic mismatch: the pattern matcher found 'key' in an env var name and flagged it as a credential. LTI Consumer Keys are platform identifiers, not authentication secrets. The actual secret (consumer secret) is stored in AWS Secrets Manager.
detection_signal: Lambda env var name contains 'key'; value: lms-platform-prod-key-2024; flagged as potential secret
ground_truth: LTI Consumer Key is a public identifier in the LTI protocol spec. It identifies the tool consumer (LMS) but provides no authentication on its own. Authentication requires the consumer secret (in Secrets Manager). Consumer keys can safely appear in configuration.
remediation_impact: Moving the consumer key identifier to Secrets Manager would complicate LTI configuration without improving security. The actual secret is already properly stored.

scenario: CloudWatch anomaly detection shows no unusual patterns for the grade submission Lambda. A student grade manipulation attack is occurring via a race condition — students are submitting concurrent requests that exploit a TOCTOU vulnerability to overwrite other students' grades. The attack is subtle (each individual request looks normal) and the anomaly detection baseline was trained on exam period high-volume data, making the current attack volume appear within normal range.
why_misclassified: EC-48 baseline contamination: the anomaly detection model was trained during finals periods with legitimately high-volume grade submissions. The attack volume during non-exam periods is lower than the trained peak, so it appears as normal variation. The attack pattern (concurrent duplicate request IDs) is not a volume anomaly.
detection_signal: CloudWatch anomaly detection: API call rate within normal bounds; no alert generated
ground_truth: Grade submission API receiving duplicate requestIds with different grade values for the same submission. Race condition allows whichever request wins to persist. 47 grade changes in 3 days outside grading periods. Pattern detectable by correlation analysis but not volume-based anomaly detection.
remediation_impact: Active grade manipulation attack. FERPA integrity violation. Fix: add idempotency tokens to grade submission API, implement distributed locking, investigate and reverse fraudulent grade changes.

scenario: Security Hub flags a security group allowing inbound SMTP (port 25) from 0.0.0.0/0 as HIGH. The instance is the university's authorized outbound mail relay. It must accept inbound SMTP on port 25 from anywhere to receive delivery status notifications and bounces from recipient mail servers worldwide.
why_misclassified: EC-06 CIDR-gated by protocol purpose: SMTP port 25 on a mail relay must accept connections from any MTA in the world. Restricting to specific CIDRs is technically impossible for a functioning mail server. This is how email routing works globally.
detection_signal: Security group allows TCP/25 from 0.0.0.0/0; instance tagged as mail-relay
ground_truth: Instance is the university's authoritative outbound MTA (Postfix). Port 25 is open for DSN reception and legitimate inbound relay. Rate limiting and DNSBL blocking applied at the application layer. SPF/DKIM/DMARC enforced.
remediation_impact: Restricting SMTP to specific CIDRs would break delivery status notification reception and prevent legitimate email bounce processing.

scenario: GCP SCC flags an OpenCourseWare legacy bucket for not having uniform bucket-level access enabled. The bucket uses object-level ACLs to allow some objects to be public (published lectures) while others remain private (draft materials). Enabling uniform access would remove all object ACLs and require IAM-only access, breaking the mixed public/private access model.
why_misclassified: EC-22 intentional ACL model: the bucket uses object-level ACLs as a deliberate access control strategy. Uniform bucket-level access would eliminate the fine-grained per-object control required for the publish/draft workflow. The current ACL model is the intended design.
detection_signal: GCS bucket iamConfiguration.uniformBucketLevelAccess.enabled=false
ground_truth: Bucket has 15,000 objects: 12,000 public (published), 3,000 private (draft). Object ACLs control the publish state. Enabling uniform access would make all 3,000 draft objects public or require migrating to a separate bucket structure.
remediation_impact: Enabling uniform bucket-level access would expose 3,000 unpublished draft lectures to public access, violating faculty's expectation of controlled publishing.

scenario: Azure Defender shows no findings for the university student health center's FHIR API. The API is for the student health center (teaching hospital component). A misconfigured FHIR search parameter allows querying patient records without specifying a patient ID — returning all records matching a diagnosis code. This enables bulk PHI extraction with a simple query.
why_misclassified: EC-51 HIPAA-specific business logic vulnerability: Azure Defender checks infrastructure configuration (auth, encryption, network). It cannot detect application-level FHIR query logic vulnerabilities. The API is properly authenticated and encrypted — the vulnerability is in the query parameter validation.
detection_signal: Azure Defender: API Management configured correctly; authentication enabled; TLS enforced; no finding
ground_truth: FHIR API allows GET /Patient?_has:Condition:patient:code=F32.9 without patient-level authorization. Returns all students with depression diagnosis codes. 847 student health records extractable with a single API call by any authenticated API user (includes all medical students with API access).
remediation_impact: HIPAA PHI breach risk. 847 student mental health records accessible to unauthorized parties. Implement FHIR patient compartment authorization — responses must be scoped to patient context.

scenario: AWS Compute Optimizer flags a video conferencing server as underutilized (3% average CPU over 30 days). The server is the backup instance for Panopto lecture recording infrastructure. It handles overflow during peak enrollment periods (September and January) and is idle during summer. The low average CPU is the desired state.
why_misclassified: EC-12 blue-green/standby pattern: the instance serves as overflow capacity for known peak periods. 3% average CPU across 30 days reflects the mix of idle standby periods and burst usage during semester starts.
detection_signal: Compute Optimizer: CPU utilization 3% average; recommendation: downsize or terminate
ground_truth: Instance tagged: role=overflow-standby, peak-months=september,january. During September peak: CPU hits 78%. During summer: CPU near 0%. Average over 30 days (in summer) is misleading. Downsizing would cause recording failures during semester start rush.
remediation_impact: Downsizing or terminating the standby recording instance would cause lecture recording failures for 800+ courses during peak enrollment period.

scenario: AWS Inspector shows no vulnerabilities for the course catalog sync Lambda. The function depends on a GitHub Actions CI/CD pipeline that pulls npm packages at build time. The CI/CD workflow file has a compromised third-party action (uses: malicious-org/setup-env@v2.1.0) that was introduced via a dependency update PR that passed automated review. The action exfiltrates environment variables (including AWS credentials) during CI runs.
why_misclassified: EC-42 supply chain via CI/CD: vulnerability is in the CI/CD pipeline, not in the deployed Lambda package. AWS Inspector scans the deployed artifact — it has no visibility into the GitHub Actions workflow that produced it. The credential exfiltration happens during build, not in the deployed function.
detection_signal: Inspector: Lambda function package scanned; 0 CVEs; all clear
ground_truth: GitHub Actions workflow .github/workflows/deploy.yml line 12: uses: malicious-org/setup-env@v2.1.0. This action was published to GitHub Marketplace 3 weeks ago. It exfiltrates secrets.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and secrets.AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY to attacker's endpoint during every CI run.
remediation_impact: AWS credentials compromised in every build for 3 weeks. Rotate all AWS credentials used in CI/CD immediately. Audit all GitHub Actions dependencies. Remove malicious action. Review what was deployed with potentially compromised credentials.

scenario: Azure Defender flags a guest user account from a partner university as HIGH because they have Contributor access to the joint research resource group. This is a visiting researcher under a formal sponsored research agreement who needs to run computational jobs on the university's Azure HPC cluster.
why_misclassified: EC-27 intra-org trust with formal agreement: the guest user's access is governed by a sponsored research agreement, scoped to a specific research resource group, and was approved via the standard external collaboration request process. Guest Contributor on a research RG is standard practice for visiting researchers.
detection_signal: Azure Entra guest user (external domain) has Contributor role on resource group
ground_truth: Guest user invited via Azure B2B with sponsor: prof.doe@university.edu. Access scoped to rg-joint-research-2025 only. Access request ticket: SRC-2025-0342 approved by CISO. Sponsored research agreement on file. Access expires 2026-05-31.
remediation_impact: Removing researcher access would halt NIH co-funded joint research project with $1.5M in active grants.

scenario: GuardDuty generates a LOW severity CryptoCurrency:EC2/BitcoinTool.B finding for a GPU compute node in the HPC cluster. The finding is automatically downgraded to LOW because GuardDuty's severity model assumes HPC GPU instances have higher baseline rates of mining-like traffic patterns (high GPU utilization, external connection patterns). A student researcher has actually installed a Monero miner on the node after compromising the cluster.
why_misclassified: EC-50 CSP enhanced controls inflating/deflating severity: GuardDuty's severity calibration for HPC GPU instances assumes mining-like patterns are normal. The automatic downgrade for 'HPC workloads' masks actual cryptomining. The finding should be HIGH given an unauthorized process is running.
detection_signal: GuardDuty: CryptoCurrency:EC2/BitcoinTool.B; auto-downgraded to LOW for HPC instance type
ground_truth: Process xmrig (Monero miner) running as PID 31337 on the GPU node. Network connections to pool.minexmr.com:4444. Unauthorized process consuming $4,200/month in GPU compute costs. Student gained access via weak SSH key from their personal laptop.
remediation_impact: Terminate unauthorized process, rotate SSH keys, investigate how student gained access to cluster nodes, file incident report. Financial impact: ~$4,200/month unauthorized compute cost.

scenario: GCP SCC flags the research HPC project for having an external user (from a @researchpartner.org domain) with roles/owner. This is the university's Google Cloud account manager who provides technical support and was given Owner for a specific troubleshooting engagement. The access was supposed to be temporary but was not removed.
why_misclassified: EC-28 break-glass / external support access: the Owner grant was made for a vendor support engagement. While this is an overpermission risk (Owner is too broad), it was an intentional grant by the university IT team. However, the failure to remove it after the engagement is a real gap that should be addressed.
detection_signal: External domain user has roles/owner on production GCP project
ground_truth: Vendor support access granted 2025-11-05 for troubleshooting session. Engagement completed 2025-11-08. Owner role was not removed. This is a real over-permission issue but the original grant was authorized. Should be downgraded to severity MEDIUM and remediated, not treated as an active breach.
remediation_impact: Remove roles/owner from vendor account immediately. Replace with time-bound, scoped support access process for future vendor engagements. Not an emergency — grant was authorized but expired.

scenario: Security Hub shows no findings for the student portal Cognito User Pool. The User Pool has MFA configured as OPTIONAL. A feature flag in the application code, REQUIRE_MFA_FOR_ADMIN=true, enforces MFA for admin-role users at the application layer. Security Hub passes the Cognito MFA check because MFA is enabled. However, the application-layer MFA enforcement has a bypass: changing the role claim in the JWT before token verification allows bypassing the admin MFA check entirely.
why_misclassified: EC-45 feature flag bypass: the infrastructure check (Cognito MFA available) passes. The application-layer enforcement contains a JWT role claim validation bug that allows privilege escalation before MFA is checked. Scanner cannot see application-layer authentication logic.
detection_signal: Cognito User Pool: MFA enabled (optional); Security Hub: pass
ground_truth: Application reads role from unverified JWT claim before checking MFA requirement. Attacker can craft a JWT with role=student, authenticate without MFA, then modify the role claim to admin in subsequent requests due to improper claim validation in the middleware.
remediation_impact: Authentication bypass to admin functions in FERPA-scoped student portal. Requires fix in JWT validation middleware: verify role claims from authoritative source (Cognito groups), not from user-controllable JWT claims.

scenario: Security Hub flags the quiz answer cache Redis cluster for not having encryption in transit enabled. The cluster is within an isolated VPC with no external access. All traffic between the application tier and the Redis cluster travels over the VPC's internal network only. The performance overhead of TLS was the reason for disabling it for this high-throughput quiz system.
why_misclassified: EC-08/EC-13 compensating control: encryption in transit is not enabled but the data never leaves the VPC's private network. TLS in-transit encryption is most important for data crossing trust boundaries. Within an isolated VPC private subnet, the risk of interception is minimal.
detection_signal: ElastiCache AtRestEncryptionEnabled=true; TransitEncryptionEnabled=false; data classification: student-activity
ground_truth: All Redis communication is within the app-tier subnet to the Redis subnet via VPC routing. No data crosses any external boundary. At-rest encryption IS enabled. VPC flow logs show only internal 10.x.x.x traffic on port 6379.
remediation_impact: Enabling transit encryption adds ~8% latency overhead on a cache handling 50,000 QPS during exams. While TLS is best practice, risk profile with VPC isolation is low. Should be addressed in next major version upgrade rather than emergency change.

scenario: GCP SCC flags a Cloud Function with allUsers:invoker permission (unauthenticated invocations allowed). The function is the inbound webhook for receiving automated data deliveries from the NSF Open Data repository. NSF's automation cannot authenticate with GCP IAM — it POSTs data with HMAC-signed payloads per the data sharing agreement.
why_misclassified: EC-40 org policy override for webhook: the function must accept unauthenticated invocations because NSF's data delivery system is external and cannot be given GCP service account credentials. HMAC signature validation on the payload provides authentication at the application layer.
detection_signal: Cloud Function invoker: allUsers; function tagged: nsf-data-ingestion
ground_truth: Function validates HMAC-SHA256 signature on every invocation (X-NSF-Signature header). Only payloads signed with the NSF shared secret are processed. Invalid signatures return 403. No sensitive data in the function — it's an inbound ingestion gateway.
remediation_impact: Requiring GCP authentication would block NSF data deliveries which cannot be given GCP credentials. Equivalent security is provided by HMAC validation.

scenario: Azure Policy compliance shows 100% compliant for the storage account SKU restriction policy (requiring Standard_LRS or Premium_LRS). The policy has an exemption for the student records storage account 'universitysistore' that was created during a migration project. The exemption comment says 'temporary: remove after migration' but was set with no expiration. The policy exemption makes the resource invisible to policy compliance reports.
why_misclassified: EC-50 / EC-49 policy exemption without expiration: the compliance dashboard shows 100% because exempted resources are excluded from compliance calculations. The exemption was intended to be temporary but became permanent by default.
detection_signal: Azure Policy compliance: 100% (all resources compliant or exempt); universitysistore: exempt
ground_truth: universitysistore is exempt from the storage SKU policy and also from related security policies (encryption, network rules). The storage account uses a non-standard SKU with weaker redundancy and is exempt from all security policy evaluation. Contains FERPA student information records.
remediation_impact: Remove policy exemption, bring storage account into compliance with security policies, establish expiration dates on all future policy exemptions.

scenario: GCP SCC shows a CRITICAL finding for a Cloud SQL instance with a publicly accessible IP. The finding was generated 120 days ago. The SQL instance was decommissioned 95 days ago as part of the Banner SIS migration to Azure SQL. The GCP project still exists (for billing audit purposes) but contains no running resources. SCC continues to show the finding as ACTIVE.
why_misclassified: EC-24 stale scan: the Cloud SQL instance no longer exists. The finding is an artifact. GCP SCC did not automatically resolve the finding when the resource was deleted because the finding pre-dates the resource deletion.
detection_signal: GCP SCC CRITICAL finding: Cloud SQL public IP; finding age: 120 days; status: ACTIVE
ground_truth: gcloud sql instances describe banner-db-prod returns 'ERROR: (gcloud.sql.instances.describe) HTTPError 404: The Cloud SQL instance does not exist.' Instance was deleted 2025-11-02. Finding is a ghost reference to a deleted resource.
remediation_impact: Mark finding as RESOLVED. No security action required. Resource does not exist.

scenario: CSPM shows no sensitive data findings for the application logs archive bucket. The bucket contains application logs which normally don't contain PII. However, a recent code change to the student portal accidentally started logging full HTTP request bodies (including form submissions) to application logs. Student login forms include username, and in some error paths, partial password data is logged. Macie has not been enabled for this bucket.
why_misclassified: EC-44 SBOM gap: CSPM checks bucket policy and encryption (both correct). Macie is not enabled for log buckets by default. The sensitive data appears in logs due to a recent application-level change that wasn't caught in code review.
detection_signal: S3 bucket: no public access; encryption enabled; no Macie findings (Macie not enabled for this bucket)
ground_truth: Application logs contain: 'POST /login body={"username":"student@univ.edu","password":"P@ss..."}' (truncated but partial password visible). Change was introduced in commit a1b2c3d, 3 weeks ago. Affects 45,000 daily login attempts. Logs retained 1 year.
remediation_impact: FERPA breach — authentication credentials in logs. Fix application code to scrub sensitive fields before logging. Enable Macie on log buckets. Assess whether existing logs need to be deleted.

scenario: GuardDuty flags reconnaissance activity from a university IP address against AWS APIs — unusually high DescribeInstances, ListBuckets calls. This activity comes from the university's own security team running their weekly automated cloud asset inventory scan using an open-source tool (Prowler) to maintain the asset management database.
why_misclassified: EC-09 dev/security tooling activity: the reconnaissance pattern is from an authorized security scanning tool run by the university security team. The high-volume API calls are legitimate asset discovery, not attacker reconnaissance.
detection_signal: GuardDuty: Recon:IAMUser/UserPermissions from IP 192.168.10.50; high-volume describe API calls
ground_truth: IP 192.168.10.50 is the security team's Prowler scanning server (documented in CMDB). Weekly scans run Monday 2am UTC. GuardDuty finding pattern matches Prowler's API enumeration pattern exactly. Security team scheduling confirmed.
remediation_impact: Suppressing this finding for the Prowler scanner IP is appropriate. Creating a GuardDuty suppression rule for the security scanning host eliminates recurring false alert.

scenario: A faculty member with administrative AWS access went on 12-month sabbatical. An IAM inactive user finding was generated and then suppressed with the note 'approved leave — account to be reactivated on return.' The sabbatical ended 4 months ago and the faculty member returned but the suppression was never removed. The account is still active, the faculty member has not used it, and no one checked whether the deactivation occurred.
why_misclassified: EC-49 suppression with future condition never re-evaluated: the suppression was appropriate when applied (sabbatical in progress) but the condition for re-evaluation (return from sabbatical) was never checked. The account may have been reactivated without the planned access review.
detection_signal: IAM user inactive finding: suppressed with reason approved-sabbatical-leave (suppressed 2025-01-15)
ground_truth: Faculty member returned 2025-09-01 (4 months ago). Account review was supposed to happen on return. IAM user has AdministratorAccess policy, console password active, no MFA. Last login: 8 months ago (pre-sabbatical). Account was never reviewed or access was never adjusted on return.
remediation_impact: Privileged IAM account with no recent use and no access review. Revoke console access pending formal access review. Re-establish appropriate permissions aligned with current role.

scenario: Azure Defender flags Azure Key Vault for not using a customer-managed key for Key Vault encryption. The Key Vault stores application secrets (database passwords, API keys). The Key Vault content IS encrypted — using Microsoft-managed keys. The finding conflates 'encrypted with Microsoft keys' (current state) with 'not encrypted' (finding title says 'no encryption').
why_misclassified: EC-39 missing CMK not missing encryption: Key Vault is encrypted at rest. Microsoft-managed keys provide real encryption. The compliance gap is the key custody model (CMK for regulatory requirements), not absence of encryption. Finding title and severity are misleading.
detection_signal: Key Vault: no customer-managed key configured; Defender title: 'Key vaults should have encryption enabled'
ground_truth: Key Vault content is encrypted with Microsoft-managed HSM keys (AES-256). Data is protected. The compliance requirement for CMK is driven by specific regulatory frameworks (FedRAMP, ITAR) that don't apply to this university. For FERPA/GLBA, Microsoft-managed keys are acceptable.
remediation_impact: Migrating to CMK adds HSM costs and operational complexity for regulatory compliance not required by this institution. Lower priority compliance improvement, not a security emergency.

scenario: No GuardDuty or Security Hub alerts for the financial aid processing account. An attacker who compromised a developer's laptop is making API calls using stolen AWS SSO credentials. The attacker is carefully mimicking the developer's normal working hours (9am-5pm EST) and API call patterns to avoid anomaly detection. The stolen credential was used from a coffee shop IP in the same city — geographic anomaly is minimal.
why_misclassified: EC-48 adversarial evasion of baseline: attacker has profiled the developer's behavior patterns and is deliberately staying within the statistical baseline for time-of-day, API call frequency, and geographic proximity. Behavioral anomaly detection cannot detect what looks statistically normal.
detection_signal: CloudTrail: normal API patterns; GuardDuty: no findings; Security Hub: no alerts
ground_truth: Attacker accessed AWS SSO from a coffee shop (same city as developer). Calls are being made 9am-4:30pm on weekdays. 95% of calls are read-only (identical to developer pattern). 5% are novel — reading financial aid S3 objects the developer never accesses. Low-and-slow exfiltration of student financial records.
remediation_impact: Active credential compromise with data exfiltration. Detection requires correlation analysis beyond baseline deviation. Implement device trust (require corporate MDM device for SSO). Investigate all S3 reads on financial aid data.

scenario: AWS Backup compliance report flags a web application EC2 instance for not having a backup plan. The instance is a stateless web node in an Auto Scaling Group — all state is stored in RDS (backed up) and S3 (versioned). The instance itself holds no data; if it fails, Auto Scaling replaces it within 3 minutes from a golden AMI.
why_misclassified: EC-05 shielded by architecture: stateless EC2 in ASG with externalized state does not require instance-level backup. The recovery mechanism is ASG replacement from AMI, not instance restoration. Backing up a stateless compute node provides no recovery value.
detection_signal: EC2 instance has no AWS Backup plan; instance tagged: prod; data classification: student-facing
ground_truth: Instance is part of ASG 'web-asg' with min=2, max=10. Launch template references golden AMI ami-0abc123. All application state in RDS (automated backup enabled, 7-day retention) and S3 (versioning enabled). Instance backup would only save the running OS state, not application data.
remediation_impact: Adding EC2 instance backup to a stateless ASG node creates unnecessary backup storage costs (~$45/month per instance) with no recovery benefit. RDS and S3 backups cover all actual data.
